subsubtopic: INCOME-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43, I seek the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
In view of the fact that the Canadian economy is in a state of complete stagnation, that industries are closing because they cannot sell their products, that unemployed workers lack the necessary money to buy products readily available and start the economy rolling again, considering that it is imperative under these circumstances to act immediately and provide consumers with the necessary purchasing power, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert):
That the House consider without further delay the possibility of establishing a guaranteed annual income for all Canadians indistinctively, for the purpose of setting in motion again the hard pressed Canadian economy.

SUGGESTED TABLING OF REPORT ON TORONTO INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT AND DELAY IN CONSTRUCTION-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43 I request the unanimous consent of the House to propose a motion on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
It concerns the reported recommendations in the Report of the Airport Inquiry Commission concerning a second international airport in Toronto. In view of the fact that the latest estimated total cost of this airport to the public is $1.5 billion, an amount which will undoubtedly increase if current inflationary pressures persist, and because both domestic and international airline associations state that [DOT] projections for future passenger and freight growth are uncertain-and made even more so by doubts about the future cost and availability of energy supplies-I would move, seconded by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald):
That the government now table the aforementioned report and refrain from taking any action thereon until such time as a clear decision can be made as to the ultimate costs, and traffic growth can be accurately determined.

subtopic: SYNCRUDE PROJECT-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO ENSURE DEVELOPMENT
SYNCRUDE PROJECT-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO ENSURE DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to put a question to the Minister
January 30, 1975

of Energy, Mines and Resources regarding the Syncrude project and the fact that the sponsors have set a deadline which expires tomorrow. In view of the fact that the National Energy Board has said that unless we get oil from the Athabasca oil sands on schedule this country will face very serious problems in respect of oil supplies in the early 1980's, and in view of the fact that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources was not able to reach any satisfactory agreement with the consortium during his meeting yesterday, I should like to ask what action the government proposes to take to ensure that the Athabasca oil sands development will be proceeded with in order that Canadians can be assured of oil supplies in the future?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: SYNCRUDE PROJECT-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO ENSURE DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps I could correct the hon. gentleman to this extent. The government of Canada has set out its position with regard to this project to the partners in Syncrude, and indicated that we would be prepared to participate in respect of additional costs along with other parties. At this point the difficulty with regard to coming in or not coming in rests with other parties, private and public, to whom the Syncrude partners have addressed themselves. The decision as to further participation does not rest at the moment in our hands.
The over-all position the government is taking is, as I said, that it will be responsible for some of the additional costs, but we do not feel that the federal public sector should have to bear the full burden. At this point while the discussions are going on, for example this afternoon, between the partners, the government of Alberta and potentially other parties, I would not draw the conclusion that a transaction may not be put together. This is really impossible to say at this point.

subtopic: SYNCRUDE PROJECT-REQUEST FOR DETAILS OF CONCESSIONS GRANTED
SYNCRUDE PROJECT-REQUEST FOR DETAILS OF CONCESSIONS GRANTED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask the minister what are the concessions the Syncrude Company has requested? I understand it has already been assured by the Minister of Finance that the project and plants will be exempt from the resource tax, but that Imperial and Gulf are also asking that they be exempt from resource taxes on all their operations and be guaranteed the international price. Are these the concessions they are asking for or are there any others they want? What concessions has the government agreed to?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: SYNCRUDE PROJECT-REQUEST FOR DETAILS OF CONCESSIONS GRANTED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Syncrude partners sought assurance on four points, on several of which they have already had assurance. The first was that production from the plant would not be pro-rated in the event of a general pro-rationing of Alberta production in the future. To the extent that the jurisdiction of the government of Canada extends, we have given them that assurance.
The second was that the interpretation of the tax law which was made known to the consortium in the fall of 1973 remains the government's view of the tax law at present, and my colleague would be in a position to con-
Oral Questions
firm that to them. My colleague has written to them, in fact, confirming that.
The third was that the price to be obtained for Syncrude oil in 1979 when the plant, all things being equal, would be in operation, would be an internationally oriented price. We have indicated to them that for the purpose of this project only, and for the purpose of attracting other participants to it, we would be prepared to agree to that price for the Syncrude product. The agreement was that they would find other participants. We have indicated that we would be prepared to undertake participation ourselves, but not total participation.
The suggestion that there should be a further tax concession to one or any of the other companies on any aspects of its operations is not one that has been put to me or, to my knowledge, to my officials. That is not under consideration.

speechtext: The officials of Syncrude have indicated that what they would prefer would be to have a participant who would take up 50 per cent of the equity. speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: SYNCRUDE PROJECT-GOVERNMENT POSITION ON FIFTY PER CENT PARTICIPATION

One of the alternatives, of course, is by way of convertible debenture which, in the event of the success of the plan, the government could convert to an equity position. I would say that other private parties to which the consortium have directed themselves would be primarily coming in as equity investors.

subtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO INDIAN ACT TO GIVE WOMEN EQUAL RIGHTS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. It has to do with the judgment rendered by the Supreme Court of Canada in the last few days in the Canard case. Under this judgment, one which certainly has reactionary implications, Indian women were declared not to have equal rights with respect to testamentary dispositions with those possessed by male Indians.
I refer to this case because a federal court earlier decided that Indian women had the same right as men in this area. The Department of Justice, not satisfied with that judgment, appealed to the Supreme Court of Canada, as they did in the Lavalle case. Is the minister, in the Year of Women, when so many protestations are made concerning the belief of members of the government in women's rights, prepared to assure us that an amendment will immediately be introduced to the Indian Act to ensure that discrimination against Indian women, as declared to be permitted, apparently, according to the judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada, will be ended once and for all?

subtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO INDIAN ACT TO GIVE WOMEN EQUAL RIGHTS-GOVERNMENT POSITION

We intend to stand by that commitment.

The House resumed, from Tuesday, January 28, consideration of the motion of Mr. Turner (Ottawa-Carleton) that Bill C-49, to amend the statute law relating to income tax, be read the second time and referred to committee of the whole.

Mr. Speaker, on Tuesday last when I was speaking on Bill C-49 I said we in the official opposition believe that further tax deductions and relief should be given to the taxpayers of Canada. We believe that there is room for a further tax deduction of 5
Income Tax
per cent in addition to the extra 3 per cent proposed by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) in the bill before us. I say this because I feel that to the extent we start limiting government revenue we will start controlling government expenditures. Our Minister of Finance has indicated that he hopes to hold government spending now to a 15 per cent increase. I noticed today, in response to a question, that he is now up to almost 16 per cent. Already the government is starting to give.
Let members of the Liberal caucus look at page 33 of the minister's budgetary papers and they will find that he is forecasting government expenditures to rise from the 1974 fiscal year level of $20 billion to the 1976 fiscal year level of $28.8 billion. It is not hard to see that that is approximately a 44 per cent increase in government spending in two years. That, I say, is an expenditure that could and should be controlled more effectively than the Minister of Finance is indicating in his figures. I suggest that hon. members look at how the government proposes to raise that revenue. I refer members of the House, particularly members of the Liberal caucus, to page 34 of the budgetary papers. There they will find, under budgetary revenues, the first item, personal income tax, which is shown as $7,926 million for the fiscal year 1974. For the fiscal year 1976 it is shown as $11,350 million. Imagine, in two years they intend to tax Canadians an extra $3.4 billion, an increase of over 40 per cent, in personal income tax alone!
If you go on to page 35, you will see that on a national accounts basis the government intends to increase direct taxation, with respect to personal income tax, from $11 billion in the fiscal year 1974 to $15.9 billion in the fiscal year 1976. This is another whopping increase, in excess of 40 per cent-an increase of almost $5 billion in direct taxation of the hard working Canadian public. Let me remind the House that if these big-spending cabinet ministers see that kind of money available, they will think up ways and means of spending it. That is why we in the official opposition say that this revenue should be cut back by at least half a billion dollars and then we would start meaningful control of government spending in this country.
The money is there. Look at the Bank of Canada figures. Right now the government is sitting on almost $5 billion that they have on deposit with the Bank of Canada and other banks. We are saying, "Give half a billion dollars of that money back to the Canadian taxpayers."
Hear, hear!

We are saying, more especially, to the Minister of Finance, or to the group of seven economic advisers-whoever is today calling the tune, economically, today in this country-"You can well afford that", and by giving this money back the government will be taking the first concrete step to ensure that we have less government expenditure, which is increasing so rapidly now. I say that because I believe the economic forecasts for the forthcoming year that are being put out by responsible organizations are alarming.
On Tuesday last I referred to the macro economic effects of federal fiscal policies for 1974-1975 issued by G. V. Jump and T. A. Wilson of the University of Toronto. Oddly enough, Mr. Wilson is one of the group of seven advising

the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on economic affairs. This is what the two gentlemen say after reviewing the effects of the November 18 budget on our economy:
It can be readily seen that Canada's economic performance for the year as a whole will clearly be inadequate in terms of the three main criteria of full employment, reasonable price stability, and adequate economic growth. With a growth rate of 2.6 per cent-about half of our potential growth rate-the unemployment rate will rise through the next few months, reaching a peak of 7 per cent in the third and fourth quarters of the year, and averaging 6.8 per cent for the year as a whole. Inflation for the year as a whole will average 11 per cent-
That is why we are stating that this government has not done enough to stimulate our economy. We believe that a further reduction of 5 per cent would help stimulate the economy, would restrain government spending and would be anti-inflationary. A reduction would have that antiinflationary effect if the funds are returned to the taxpayer rather than if the government retained the money and spent it on some of its fanciful programs. To be specific, when I am suggesting a $500 million deduction for Canadian taxpayers, I am speaking about a deduction that in 1975 would amount to a $60 to $150 tax reduction for most taxpayers in this country. I feel they deserve it. We need that kind of consumer spending power to be put back into the economy. I implore members of this House to press the government to be more generous with the taxpayers and less inclined to hold taxpayers' money so that they can spend it as freely as they have been spending it.

Mr. Speaker, I am not going to reinforce the Cassandra-like utterances of the hon. member who preceded me, because I think that while we will have some difficulties in the coming year despite the best efforts of the government, the country will do all right. I think the economy is essentially strong and healthy and not even the government can damage it very much. It seems to me that the simple problem we have to face in this budget is how to balance one thing off against the other. There has been a great deal of argument about this. I was trying to follow the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens). I could not see how the reduction he suggested would stimulate the economy and at the same time reduce inflation. I was having difficulty following that argument.
It seems to me that the central problem is one that we have consistently pointed out from this side of the House, and that is the distribution of income amongst various sectors of the economy. In that regard this budget, like so many of the budgets preceding it, is enormously regressive in the way that benefits are being passed on. For instance, in the last two or three budgets the minister brought in a long list of the number of people who were being knocked off the income tax rolls. He has managed to knock more people off the income tax rolls than we have people in Canada. Yet somehow people go on paying income tax.

I wonder if I could ask the hon. gentleman a question. I wonder how he reconciles that statement with the statement he made with regard to the last budget, that it was the most progressive in history with regard to tax cuts.

I am not quite sure what the minister's question was. I am not sure where his budget is going, either. I am going to give one example of the kind of thing which masquerades as progressiveness in the minister's budget. When he came out with the opportunity for people to set aside money in a registered retirement savings plans and then to draw from it later on, it sounded great on the surface. But who benefits? How many ordinary people in this country are able to put $1,000, $2,000 or $3,000 into a registered retirement savings plan every year, or into a registered home ownership plan? Not very many.
Mr. Asper, whose credentials I think are reasonably good in the Liberal Party, had something to say about this in a column he wrote recently. I think the implication of his column is that until now we have had a great bonanza for tax consultants in industry finding all kinds of generous little opportunities from which they could benefit. Now we are going to extend this advantage to those who have money and may not be in business as such. Now they are going to be afforded great opportunities for tax dodges whereby they do not have to pay any money out of their savings. I quote from the article which Mr. Asper wrote in the Ottawa Journal of December 2:
The most fertile area for planning is the amendment which allows each individual the right to earn up to $1,000 per year of investment, income tax free. For the 1974 year, the only investments which qualify are interest-bearing securities of banks, trust companies, mortgages, bonds and the like.
But for the 1975 year, dividends from taxable Canadian companies will also receive the tax free treatment. In all cases, the interest or dividend must be paid by someone with whom the taxpayer deals at arm's length. Thus, dividends from the family business, or interest on most shareholder loans to family companies, won't qualify.
It then pays the private business operator to have his company borrow, say, $10,000 from its banker, repay his shareholder loan, or pay him a dividend, and personally invest the money in tax free interest earning securities. The interest his company pays on the borrowed money is deductible while the interest he earns personally is tax free.
But that is not the end of the benefits.
Since the courts have ruled that a father can loan money interest free to his wife and children, provided the money is repayable on demand, family investment portfolios might be reorganized to improve the group's protection against erosion of the value of the unit's savings.
If the father has an investment portfolio of $50,000 earning interest at 10 per cent-
You will notice, Mr. Speaker, that he is referring to the typical Canadian family, the average family.
-he would earn $5,000, of which $1,000 is tax free and $4,000 is taxable. If, instead, he kept only $10,000 and loaned $10,000 to each of his wife and three children, and they invested at 10 per cent, the entire $5,000 of interest would be tax free.
The budget also offers tax planning incentives for those who are willing to save money through registered retirement savings plans.
He goes on to fault a few of the other benefits which the average Canadian taxpayer can claim. Those are typical of the things that appear in the budget. The budget is to a large extent a method of redistribution of income, and I have seen no evidence of a fair-minded attitude toward the redistribution of income in this country. It seems every time there is a suggestion that Canada may be going into a recession and we have to increase demand, the tendency is to give the benefits to the people at upper income levels rather than to pass them on to the lower levels. This is one of the criticisms of the minister's budget which I think he must accept.

There is one major area which, at the time the budget came in in its original form in May of 1974, attracted very little attention. I refer to the provision for disallowing oil royalty payments before federal taxation. It seems to me that the government is being terribly sneaky. It is guilty of lack of frankness with the Canadian people in telling them what is ahead. In fact, the government has already made a deal to raise the price of oil substantially in this country in order to get itself out of some serious difficulties. The only thing it is trying to do is box the provinces in and make them look like the villains of the piece when in fact it is the federal government which must shift its methods of taxation from the export tax to the corporate tax in order to take care of the deficit and the one-price system in the eastern provinces.
The government knows what is happening and it is preparing itself, by this method, to maintain the one-price system. My criticism is this. It may be necessary for the government to move in this direction. It may be necessary for royalty payments beyond a certain point to be disallowed. But it is not necessary for the government to take with both hands; to take an export tax with one hand and then to take, by disallowing royalty payments, with the other. What is not acceptable is the way the federal government has approached this issue and imposed strains on confederation. That is not necessary.
Had there been more frankness and openness about the problem facing the federal government and the need to share and redistribute this income, much of the ill-feeling that has been engendered would have been avoided. When you watch the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) these days, you have the impression that you are seeing a rerun of an old movie. If old movies are given four stars for a great movie, and one star for something which is not so great, I think this one would receive an apostrophe because it is so bad. It is one of those movies where you recognize the players because you have seen them before. You recognize the plot. Of course, there is a plot, you know that, but you are not quite sure how the movie is going to end, so you are watching it to see if you can identify the elements which tell you what the ending is. You look at the cast, and enter on the left the heroic figure of the Minister of Finance, the knight in shining armour, holding the pass like Leonidas at Thermopylae and saying, "The provinces shall not pass. We shall defend federal rights." He is the hero of all the people.
Enter the villains, as the minister has painted them the provincial premiers, protesting their innocence, saying that they have been shafted and this is not what they had laboured over. Then, of course, there is a fade-back a number of years and you realize it is not quite what the Minister of Finance, the knight in shining armour is saying. That is what fade-backs are: the good becomes bad and the bad becomes good, and it all gets very confused. You find they are really not much different. All you have is a bunch of people fighting over the apportionment of this pile of income. Then you remember how the movie ends: it all comes back to you. You remember the saloon scene and the two antagonists with guns drawn, ready to shoot it out. They then turn carefully and shoot the piano player. That is exactly what both of them intend to do at the present time, the piano player being the Canadian consumer.

I am persuaded, both by some of the things that the minister has said in his speeches and by the events that have taken place, that the provinces and the federal government have concluded a deal, if not in fact at least in principle, to raise the price of oil to consumers. In that way the provinces would get what they want, the federal government would get what it wants, and the consumers would pay for it. One province will get a slice anyway, but I do not know that Saskatchewan will get very much consideration.
When the occasion has called for it I have been as critical of the provinces as of the federal government, but I think we have to understand the position of the provinces. They have stepped into a vacuum created by the federal government. We have to go back to the time when this House and its committees were considering the white paper on taxation. I should like to think that the minister of finance of that day, Mr. Edgar Benson, seriously wanted tax reform. But what was the consequence? The word was out that the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton, the present Minister of Finance, was not very sympathetic toward tax reform. Certainly the Liberal backbenchers were the worst enemies of the minister of finance of that day; piece by piece they eroded the meagre tax reforms that were being introduced, not the least of which was taxation of the oil companies. The federal government backed off any attempt to tax the oil companies.
When the price of oil rose, the province of Saskatchewan had a choice: it could let the oil companies apportion the entire amount if they wanted to, or it could move in to fill that oversight of the federal government. This is what it proceeded to do, but then the federal government realized its commitment to the oil industry was going to put it in a bad light, so it got progressive too and moved into the field. That is how we ended up with the present confrontation.
I referred to the fact that the dilemma was resolved by shooting the piano player. The price of oil was around $3.60 or $3.80 a barrel. After we were assured it was going to remain there, it was permitted to rise to $6.50 a barrel. The consumer paid more, but at that time oil exports to the United States were heavy and the federal share of the export tax was sufficient to cover the deficit between the exported oil and oil being imported into eastern Canada. I should like to turn now to another question that arises from the federal budget, if only because the budget did not really deal with it adequately. I refer to the need for an incomes policy in this country. It is not as though we have not had an incomes policy in this country, because every

budget is in some ways an incomes policy. We have always had one. We have had an incomes policy that permitted the resource industries to make profits without paying taxes. Every time we bring in an old age pension scheme, family allowance program, corporate tax, industry subsidy, tariff or even a settlement for members of parliament, it is an incomes policy.
The time has come for this government to provide some direction. I do not suggest for a moment that this will be easy or quick. For example, the hon. member to my right spoke about a wage and price control policy for a six-month period-a six-month freeze. We can forget about things like that; they will not work. The Canadian people correctly rejected it because they could see it was not going to work. An incomes policy is not something you wave a wand over and keep for six months. It is something by which you make a commitment for the future. It is a philosophical question, one of income distribution and one that must be approached with caution. Nevertheless, it is one that has to be started.
It has often been argued that labour will not go for an incomes policy. In some ways I can understand the hesitancy of labour in the past to go for an incomes policy, because almost invariably it was labour that was hurt. It is rather interesting to see what is happening now. One of the most progressive elements is, in fact, organized labour. This has always been the case. One of the finest speeches on this subject was made by Joe Morris, president of the Canadian Labour Congress. The speech is of such merit that I should quote it, if not in its entirety at least that part which refers to his attitude toward an incomes policy. This is his New Year's message:
The challenge to the labour movement in the year ahead is to drive hard to protect men and women workers against the blight of inflation, to stop the merciless attack on the purchasing power of their hard-earned wages and salaries.
Apart from the hardship inflation poses to wage and salary earners, pensioners and, in general, all middle-and lower-income groups, there is a definite danger that the problem may, if it is not curbed soon, destroy the very social fabric of our country and other countries almost as radically and surely as violent revolution.
On the international level, the danger is that countries will take steps to protect themselves without any consideration for the damage such isolationist steps may cause other countries and the world as a whole.
In Canada, individual groups may tend to look out for their own interests alone in order to protect themselves from the dangers of inflation, often unconcerned or simply unaware that by doing so they are hurting other groups, thereby ultimately hurting themselves.
Such a return to the law of the jungle may become so divisive and destructive to the social conscience of individuals and groups alike that the things Canadians now share in common may deteriorate and, with them, the orderly and generally peaceful manner in which we live and conduct our affairs.
With them may also go the moral obligation, the understanding and the compassion which our society, if it values itself, must have for all its disadvantaged people.
The Canadian Labour Congress recognizes the dangers of inflation. Most of us realize that these dangers are not temporary but something that will not leave in our lifetime. We will not only have to live with them but deal with them. Yet in the minister's budget very little thought was given to this serious problem. The government's

At a time like this, when the government is asking for restraint, I cannot understand how they could put this kind of package together. I hear that the Minister of Finance liked the package. He said he could sell it to the Canadian public on the basis that we are getting less than other people, only 5 Vi per cent a year over eight years. Who else gets that kind of package? If we intend to move in the direction of an incomes policy, we should start with members of parliament. We should not be setting our own income. At the very least, some kind of board should make that determination. Over the years this party has called for a prices review board which could examine the demands being made in the various sectors of the economy, whether demands for profits, prices of services or prices of goods. Now is the time to set up that kind of board. Its first item of business should be the salaries of MPs. The last thing parliament should do is vote its own salaries. People say that is hypocrisy, we will take the money; we are just talking to make headlines. People will in no way accept that kind of argument. I am in no way proving I am not hypocritical. Either you accept it or you don't. All members must realize that members cannot raise their salaries to this level and maintain credibility in the country. They cannot expect anyone to ever again pay attention to what we say about wage and income restraints.
As difficult as an incomes policy or restraint policy may be, we have entered into it and will continue along that path. When you introduce a two-price system for oil, you establish an incomes policy. When you establish a two-price system for wheat, you determine the income of the wheat farmer. Therefore, it cannot be said that this is something new. We have in fact been doing this, but in a mish-mash manner. In many ways it has been so unfair that the whole concept of an incomes policy has to some extent been discredited. Looking to future politics in Canada, I do not think the debate will be whether this country is to have an incomes policy; it will be about distribution of income within an incomes policy. Parties will be judged on the basis of how they stand, to whom the income is distributed and in what fashion. That will be one of the chief debates of the future.
I have not dealt with many of the specifics in the budget because most of it is window-dressing. It is not of great value except to a select few. I am more concerned about some of the underlying principles of this budget and trying to relate them. It is important that we see a budget

Mr. Speaker, I would also like to say a few words about Bill C-49. This bill tends to drastically alter the provisions dealing with private and corporate income tax. This bill introduces new regulations concerning the new structure of corporations with respect to foreign income.
I think these amendments to the statute law relating to income tax are important to eke out the present act. However, we do not think those income tax reductions are sufficient under present economic circumstances-inflation and unemployment. With a further income tax reduction, we might have lower prices and costs and ipso facto fight the present inflationary trend.
I believe the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) is sincere, but I wonder if he is really able to manage that. He will have to improve the income tax legislation. First of all, he should raise the basic exemption from $1,000 to $6,000. This would reflect the national output which amounted to $137 billion in 1974.
Looking at statistics for earlier years, find that in 1926 for instance, the GNP was $5.15 billion, which amounted to $550 revenue per capita. Tax exemption was then $1,500.
Looking at 1940, a war year where the national product reached $6.75 billion, or $600 per capita, there was a tax deductible amount of $750. In 1969, with a national product of $78 billion, that is $3,700, per capita, the tax exemption was $1,000.
And coming to 1974, with a $137 billion GNP or $6,000 per capita, the exemption is still $1,000.
I therefore think that to keep pace with the GNP the tax deduction should be at least $6,000.
Along with other statistics, this comparison based on the number of adult working people shows how much the individual is being increasingly deprived of his personal revenues, as the cost of living increases. Such is the trend given to the economy by human decisions either in government or in big corporations.
At first, the income tax deduction was roughly three times the average per capita GNP. From 1955 to 1965, half or one-third of the average personal income is exempted, and in 1970 only approximately a quarter of the per capita GNP is exempted.
As you can see, Mr. Speaker, a readjustment in tax deduction from $1,000 to $6,000 would be very welcome now by the taxpayer with a family, and every worker facing a day-to-day erosion of his revenues through inflation.
Let us now turn to corporations which, in the period from 1957 to 1966, made $45,112 billion in declared and taxed profits. However, besides that, under profit, hidden and untaxable capital, one finds figures of $96 billion and a few millions. Untaxed profit, capital. That is why compa-

Mr. Speaker, as we know, the purpose of the bill before us is to implement changes in personal and corporate income tax proposed in the budget of November 18. Today I intend to make some comments and raise some questions about several aspects of the bill and a number of related policy areas. I want to begin by saying that I think the budget is on the right track. Therefore, my questions and comments, though at times critical in tone, are intended to be a positive and constructive nature in the context of my support, generally speaking, for the budget proposals.
In my view, the proposals are the kind required to deal with today's economic situation, marked as it is with both inflation and slower growth. Their policy thrust recognizes correctly the disturbing signs of economic slowdown in the Canadian economy and the signs of even greater slowdown in the United States and world economies- something of great concern to Canada, dependent as it is on external trade for its well-being. Therefore, I generally agree with and support what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) has said about the broad approach that is required and which is reflected in his budget and in the bill. The "first essential" of this approach, he said, is "action to sustain demand".
For this purpose the bill proposes further cuts in personal income tax. While these are helpful and are therefore welcome, it must be said that the measure does nothing for those Canadians whose income is already below the level subject to taxation. The budget speech says a married wage-earner with two children pays no federal income tax in 1974 on an income below $4,830. However, it is the low income earner who is hit hardest by inflation, especially when it comes to increases in the cost of food and increases in other basic expenses. The proposed tax cuts would mean that from 1974 to 1975 a married taxpayer with two children, earning $6,000, would have an increase in take-home pay of $214, but if that same taxpayer earned $30,000 he would have an increase in his take-home pay of $622.

This bill and the budget seem to be saying that inflation hits the higher income person harder than the one earning a low income. But surely it is just the opposite. Lower income people spend a greater proportion of their income on food than those earning more. Therefore, why should a man earning $6,000 be given only $214 more, while the man earning $30,000 will be given $622 more through tax reductions? This is done in both cases to meet "part of the increase in the cost of food". This is the purpose of the tax cut, according to the budget speech.
The bill proposes that no one would get a tax reduction of less than $200 or more than $750; that is, the cut would have a floor of $200 and a ceiling of $750. One could ask, therefore, why the proposal did not call for a higher floor and a lower ceiling. In other words, why was there not a higher minimum tax reduction and a lower maximum tax reduction to ensure that the lower and middle-income Canadian would get even more disposable income through tax reductions and the imbalance toward the higher income earner would be less than it would otherwise be?
One could also ask why, as another alternative, the proposal was not for a single, across the board tax cut of an amount somewhat higher than the minimum $200 available to all below a certain income. The latter approach would be even more progressive in the sense of giving less, proportionately, to the highest income people than the floor and ceiling approach which is being used in the budget and in this bill.
I have said that the tax cuts proposed in the November 18 budget do nothing for those whose incomes are below the level subject to tax. This point is now especially important because of the unfortunate signs of economic weakness which were noted in the budget speech but have become even more evident since it was pronounced. Thousands of people who were working and who earned enough income in 1974 to be subject to tax will not have taxable incomes, or the incomes will be severely reduced, in 1975. This is because they will be unemployed or working shorter hours this year.
Therefore, the benefits for them of the additional tax cuts proposed in the November 18 budget will be, if not non-existent then at least severely reduced. They will, of course, benefit from the smaller tax cuts announced in the May budget which apply to the 1974 tax year and have been reintroduced. There is a strong argument, therefore, to have the additional tax cuts for 1975, or a substantial portion of them, apply retroactively to 1974. This would put additional disposable income in the hands of Canadians now and over the next few months as they file their returns for 1974 and receive the tax refunds for which they will be eligible. This will be helpful especially for those who will not be earning taxable income in 1975 to the same extent as they did in 1974 because of the weakness in the Canadian and world economies.
The Minister of Finance in his November budget speech in effect noted the likelihood of higher unemployment in 1975 when he forecast the creation of 225,000 new jobs in 1975, as contrasted with the 390,000 new jobs which were created in 1974.

As I have mentioned, the budget says the proposed additional tax reduction is to pay for "a large part of the increase in the cost of the family's food over the last 12 months". However, this means that this benefit is received in arrears. How will it make up for the food a lower-income family did not purchase during this period because it simply could not pay for it out of current income, and could not borrow the money? How will it make up for the extra cost of any additional debt the family incurred to pay for food? Also, if the tax cut is for the increase in the cost of food over the past 12 months, how will it help meet the increases in food costs the budget statement indicates will be coming during the next 12 months and which have come since the date of the budget?
These questions indicate that there is still a place for other programs in addition to these tax reductions to help sustain demand-to strengthen purchasing power-by Canadians, especially lower-income Canadians. When I spoke in the throne speech debate I said that when it came to cutting government expenditure, the elimination of the subsidy on fluid milk was not the place to start. This is because of the additional burden this action puts on Canadian families and their children, particularly those in the lower income category. I pointed out that both the Food Prices Review Board and the Consumers' Association of Canada had called and continue to call for the government to continue the subsidy. I said that no one in the government concerned with the consumer interest had spoken up publicly in support of the stand of the Food Prices Review Board and the Consumers' Association. This continues to be the case even though the price of milk has been going up due to the elimination of the subsidy.
The government's response to the request of the board and the Consumers' Association to continue this subsidy was that it was unnecessary because of recent increases in social welfare benefits. One minister suggested we could drink more powdered milk since it is cheaper than fluid milk. Another minister suggested, I hope facetiously, that people, apparently including babies, could drink wine instead of milk. Of course, if there were to be a massive shift by consumers from fluid milk to powdered milk, the effects of this could very well be harmful both to the consumer and the dairy farmer. And this is entirely aside from the fact that the price of powdered milk itself has gone up in the past in spite of a federal subsidy on it.
The farmer, I understand, gets a lower return for milk put into powdered form. Therefore, if there were to be an extensive move by consumers to use powdered milk instead of fluid milk, thousands of dairy farmers likely could no longer afford to stay in business unless the price of powdered milk were allowed by the government to rise to the level of the price of fluid milk. This would mean either that consumers would have to pay a greatly increased price for powdered milk, or the government would have to pay greatly increased subsidies to farmers

to ensure they get the returns they need while at the same time holding down its price to a reasonable level for consumers.
As I pointed out before, the government did not cancel the subsidy on fluid milk immediately upon the increases in family allowance and old age security going into effect. Actually, in his pre-election budget speech of last May, the Minister of Finance referred to the subsidy on milk, along with that on bread, as being part of the government's "strategy against inflation" to "dampen down the price of particular products where this is feasible", and he said that this was done to "help all Canadian consumers". He gave no indication on behalf of the government that the fluid milk subsidy would not be continued indefinitely, in spite of its initial one-year term.
I should point out here that giving the fast write-off on production machinery and initial two-year term, such that it would have ended this year, did not prevent the government from quite correctly proposing in the new budget the indefinite extension of this measure.
The budget of last May made it clear that having subsidies on bread and milk was one element among a number of concurrent elements in the government's strategy against inflation. These included easing "the burden of those Canadians who are most vulnerable" to inflation by increases in social welfare payments and the indexing of these payments. The Minister of Finance stated specifically in his November 18 budget speech that both of these elements and the other elements of the government's strategy against inflation set out in the May 6 budget "continue to be" his "objectives" and therefore, I presume, those of the government as well. His current budget statement described the two elements in question in the following words:
-maintaining the real income of these Canadians least able to protect themselves against the cost of living... moderating the prices of certain products of importance to Canadian families.
These were not put forward last May, nor are they put forward now by the Minister of Finance, as being in any way inconsistent with or as substitutes for each other. Furthermore, I think the continuing of the subsidy on fluid milk and having similar subsidy programs to restrain the cost of other basic commodities is entirely consistent with the finance minister's approach to the important issue of the limitation of government expenditures. Here is what he said about this in his budget speech of November 18:
We must do all that we can in these circumstances to restrain the growth of governmental expenditures, particularly those which do not contribute directly to an increased supply of goods and services, that do not help those Canadians least able to protect themselves, or that do not directly moderate price increases.
His words show that subsidies to restrain the price of basic commodities for consumers should not be among those government expenditures whose growth must necessarily be restrained or eliminated, since they "help those Canadians least able to protect themselves" and they can "directly moderate price increases". Therefore, I think there should be greater convergence between what the Minister of Finance quite correctly said in his last two budget speeches about the need to help Canadians deal

An illustration of what appears to be a contradiction in government policy in this area is that while the government cancelled the subsidy on fluid milk last August, a few months later, last December, it created what amounts to a new subsidy program for beef, specifically to improve returns to beef producers and also, supposedly and hopefully, to reduce the likelihood of retail beef prices going up sharply for consumers over the coming months. It also increased the subsidy on powdered milk. Increases in social welfare benefits were not put forward by the government as substitutes for these measures.
The government cancelled the subsidy on fluid milk, but last fall the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) apparently proposed, according to numerous press reports, that a new government board should be set up to buy Canada's requirements of sugar in bulk from major sugar exporting countries. This is puzzling, to say the least. I say this because while fluid milk is one of our healthiest and most complete foods, sugar, on the other hand, according to experts on nutrition, is not only unnecessary for sound diets but is actually harmful to health, at least when consumed in sizeable quantities.
However, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and the government did not tell Canadians to rely on social welfare benefits to meet the increased cost of sugar, as they did for milk. Instead, according to columnist Richard Gwyn, the minister proposed that a "national sugar purchasing board" be set up to buy Canadian requirements of sugar from the governments of sugar exporting countries and this board would then sell it to Canadian refiners. One could ask why, when we are trying to hold down government expenditure, we would want to set up another board and another layer of bureaucracy? If there was a valid case to be made for buying our sugar in this way, last fall or at present, we already have the facilities to do this through our Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and our Department of Supply and Services. If there should be a government board to buy sugar, why not a board to buy the fruits, vegetables and other foods we have to import from abroad, the prices of which have also been going up?
What would such a sugar purchasing scheme have accomplished? Would it have enabled Canadian consumers to pay lower prices for refined sugar then or in the future? It is highly unlikely that this would have been the result. The price for raw sugar in world markets last fall was at an all-time high, as was the world demand for sugar. No country would have wanted to enter into a long-term agreement with Canada to supply sugar at less or much less than world prices at that time. Why should any country have done so? It could then have sold all it had at top world prices, or close to them, and no sugar producing country had inventories it was having difficulty getting rid of at those prices; quite the contrary. However, "Business Week" said, in its issue of last November 16:
The price of sugar is expected to decline 50 per cent within a year on world markets.
In fact, since then there have already been declines in Canadian wholesale and world prices of sugar. The Food

Prices Review Board said the major component in the causes of increases in the retail price of sugar in Canada has been the increase in the price of raw sugar on world markets, that is, markets outside our borders. So if Canada had entered into any long-term agreement last fall, it would have committed itself to buying at very high world prices, at the top of the market. It would have locked Canadian consumers into paying very high retail prices for refined sugar for many years to come and well after world prices for raw sugar were likely to have broken.
However, the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs proposal outlined in Mr. Gwyn's column went on to say that at the very least, if this new board bought all our requirements for sugar from supplying countries, "we would know the prices that Canadian refineries pay and so the price at which they should sell". We do not need a new board and more bureaucracy to obtain this information. Our Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce was, and is, quite capable of getting any available information on world prices of sugar, and it has very likely been doing this. Also, the Food Prices Review Board already has all the authority of a royal commission to find out and report publicly to consumers and the government just how much profits the Canadian refiners really make and just how much they have actually been marking up the price of the sugar they refine over what they pay for it in its raw form.
The only thing the government does not have as yet is any means of doing anything to change or roll back the prices of sugar in Canada if it finds refiners or retailers are charging Canadians unwarranted prices. In other words, what we do not have as yet on our law books is the anti-profiteering bill I proposed to parliament before the last election. This is a measure that would enable the government to deal swiftly with Canadian sugar refiners or any other industry if their prices were found to be unwarranted and if they were found, therefore, to be gouging the Canadian consumer.
High prices for sugar is a matter of understandable concern for consumers. I agree with those who say that reducing sugar consumption is a good means not only of preserving good health but also, as events have proven, a way of putting downward pressure on sugar prices in Canada. In addition, if existing agencies of government can in fact negotiate now a long-term agreement to purchase raw sugar at prices that are lower, not only than those prevailing at present but lower than or at least equal to prices likely to prevail over the next several years, of course they should proceed to do so as soon as possible.
There may also be a place for an expanded domestic sugar beet industry if this could be accomplished without locking consumers indefinitely into unduly high prices for refined sugar. But the government should not, in an attempt to reduce consumer concern over high sugar prices or other food prices, take any hasty steps which would turn out to mean, not low but high prices for an indefinite period for Canadians.
There appears to have been lack of a sufficiently coherent and co-ordinated approach within the federal government to the problem of high sugar prices. This leads one to an awareness of the need for a better approach by federal government policy to the production and marketing of all

kinds of food, particularly those kinds which can be grown in Canada. The necessity for a new approach like this is underscored by a point made by the Minister of Finance in his budget speech. Speaking of the demand for energy and food, he said:
On a world scale, it is not just an economic problem. It is a moral issue, because for many people and for many countries it is survival which is at stake. Many countries haven't enough energy to meet the basic needs of their people. Millions of people haven't enough to eat. For Canadians this is not a question of economics; it is a matter of conscience.
Canada is one of the few countries capable today of exporting a sizeable quantity of food beyond the needs of its own population. The current world food crisis and our own needs mean, therefore, that what we must have is not simply a better agricultural policy but, instead, a new total food policy. By this I mean one that integrates on a systems basis all of our presently existing separate, disjointed and often conflicting policies in this area. The responsibility for this is currently divided among a number of government departments. It must also mean the development of new policy elements in areas where they do not, but should, exist at present and their integration with existing ones. Such a total food policy must cover all aspects of the food chain; the producer, the processor, the wholesaler, the retailer, and the consumer no less than any of these.
The federal government at present has little in the way of programs to improve the efficiency and productivity of the wholesale and retail distribution of food. Also, no government department has any clear jurisdiction assigned to it for developing and implementing these kinds of policies. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) has been saying that he wants farmers to produce to beat the band. But there are already in place national and provincial agricultural marketing schemes based on quotas-that is to say, they are based on restriction of production-and more are being contemplated. The Minister of Agriculture has chastised consumers about the amount of food allegedly wasted by being left on their dinner tables. But I think we should also look at the possibility that waste of food is encouraged by the Department of Agriculture's own food grading system. This is certainly the impression created by reports like the one which appeared in the Montreal Star last fall. That story indicated that Rene Guinois, a farmer of Hemingford, Quebec-

it is time we had a thorough examination of this food grading system and parallel provincial systems, followed by any necessary changes in them. This should be done to make sure that they do not prevent food which is healthy and nutritious, although not of prime appearance, being made available at lower cost for use directly by Canadian consumers and by people in other countries as well.
Here is another example showing why there needs to be urgent and intensive work done by the federal government to develop a comprehensive national food policy. In his announcement in the House on Friday, January 24, the Minister of Agriculture said that the government was increasing the price of butter for consumers by 5 cents a pound. His justification for this was that since-
-the price of margarine has gone up substantially in the last twelve months ... this will tend to restore the competitive position between the two products.
How can increasing the price of a product restore its competitive position? Most people would say such a step would have just the opposite effect. Ordinarily, when one wants to make a product more competitive, one reduces its price, or at least one holds it at the same level as the products it is vying with for consumer acceptance. Margarine has always been cheaper than butter and it continues to be cheaper. If one really wanted to make butter more competitive with margarine-that is, to encourage people to buy more butter and less margarine-most people would say the logical answer would have been to reduce the price of butter, or at least keep it at the same level as before. After all, as of January 17 there were 30.5 million pounds of butter in storage, about a million pounds more than a year ago. The increase in price announced by the Minister of Agriculture may well encourage people to buy less, and not more, butter. Canadians can well wonder about a government decision which was presented under the guise of making butter more competitive but which results in higher, not lower, prices for consumers. The agriculture minister's announcement in effect attempts to turn the law of supply and demand upside down.
If the world food situation is as serious as it appears to be, there is indeed a case to be made for having government policies that encourage maximum production of food in Canada no matter what domestic and world market conditions may be. However, a number of problems would have to be resolved in moving in this direction. A basic question is simply to what extent our country can afford such a policy. Farmers would rightly insist on fair returns for their produce even when market prices dropped drastically because of surpluses. Such a policy would involve the cost, not only of ensuring adequate returns for farmers but also of paying for the stockpiling of surpluses and allowing sales to be made for what may have to be very low prices to less fortunate countries. Consumers would ask that the burden of this be borne primarily by government expenditure, rather than having this come almost entirely from higher food prices in the Canadian marketplace.
But to what extent could government revenues at any point in time handle all this? What, then, is the proper balance between having the cost of maximum production come from the marketplace as distinct from government expenditure? Again there is the basic question as to

January 30, 1975
Income Tax
whether Canadians will believe they can afford this cost no matter how it is divided. We will have to find sound answers to these kinds of questions if we are to move to a policy of maximum production of food at all times in order to deal, not only with our needs but also to enable Canada to play its part in helping to solve the world food crisis.
A coherent, total food system policy approach would certainly mean better ways of getting foods so long as they are safe and nutritious and even if they are not of top appearance, directly onto the tables of lower-income Canadians through new kinds of government programs. I think this would mean creating food stamp and surplus disposal programs for Canada similar to those in existence for a number of years in the United States. Under the food stamp program in that country, stamps are provided at no cost to unemployable people receiving social welfare benefits. They are provided at a low cost that is considerably less than their face value to those who might be described as working poor. The stamps can then be redeemed for their face value for food at any participating retailer. Under the surplus disposal program, foodstuffs are distributed to non-profit community agencies and institutions like day care centres, meals-on-wheels programs and homes for the aged.
I believe we can learn from the American experience and develop programs of this type for Canada that would eliminate many of the problems associated with them in that country. But I think that these kinds of programs, whatever their administrative difficulty, would be preferable to policies that possibly encourage destruction of food for alleged lack of markets or spoilage through faulty storage rather than enabling it to be placed on the tables of Canadian consumers, particularly those with low incomes.
We have been working out a coherent, long-term energy policy. It is now no less urgent to work out a coherent, total Canadian food policy. Our own needs and those of the world call out for this kind of action. However, I think that we should begin developing and putting in place the kind of food stamp and surplus disposal programs I have mentioned without waiting for a total food policy to be implemented. These kinds of programs, along with subsidy programs to restrain increases in the prices of basic commodities, would be consistent with the views expressed in the budget statement as to the kinds of government expenditure that should not necessarily have to be restrained. After all, government revenues remain strong and there are at the same time increasing and disturbing signs of recession in our economy.
As I said during the throne speech debate, putting into law both stages of a reformed competition policy is an essential way of enabling the government to deal directly with the larger concentrations of private economic power which can add to inflationary pressures on prices. In this way we would not have to rely solely on monetary and fiscal policies, constructive though those policies may be, as exemplified by the proposals in the new budget. It is important, therefore, that the government move ahead to get an updated competition law passed as soon as possible.

Also, I believe that it continues to be essential at this time, for these kinds of reasons, for the government to present the anti-profiteering bill to parliament for decision and implementation as soon as possible. I think it may well be of concern to many Canadians to recall that the need to pass this bill at a very early date was stressed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and Liberal candidates generally during the election campaign as one of the prime reasons for the re-election of the government. They said then, and have said since, that the prime reason for that bill not already being law was the election campaign, forced by the actions of the opposition parties who opposed both the May budget and the anti-profiteering bill. Although the Canadian people accepted this argument, re-elected the government, and it has been back in office for some months with a clearly majority, the bill has not yet been reintroduced into the House even for first reading.
A majority, but not a very clear one.

The November 18 budget, unlike the May 6 budget, makes no mention of the anti-profiteering bill. The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs says that the bill is "window-dressing" and he hopes that he will never have to use it, according to interviews given to the Financial Post and the Financial Times. However, I believe the Canadian people did not re-elect this government to have this important measure treated as window-dressing. They expect prompt carrying out of the government's commitment in the election to have the measure made into law as soon as possible, and once it is law, to have the will to use it whenever required.
This anti-profiteering bill, in my view, fits in well with the total approach of the new budget and the economic circumstances we are facing. This approach aims at dealing at one and the same time with the problems of inflation and recession. The budget statement refers to the existence of structural causes of price increases. What is the situation to which the budget proposals and the bill before us have to apply? It is one in which economic slack could mean that some profits and prices are falling, while at the same time concentrations of private economic power continue, in spite of pressures of the marketplace, to be able to maintain prices and profits at what could be unwarranted levels.
In my view, therefore, side by side with monetary policy and with the fiscal policy proposed by the new budget and in this bill the government needs to have the kind of weapon for a more direct attack on the structural causes of inflation that the anti-profiteering bill would provide. There is aslo need for a general review of government policies to identify the ones which build structural rigidities into our economy which help to keep up prices. I think a special parliamentary committee would be a most appropriate vehicle for this kind of review.
In this new budget and in this bill the government has shown indications of translating into action the great potential it has of meeting the commitment it gave to the Canadian people during the election campaign. The commitment was that if re-elected, the government would go on to put into effect sound and humane policies serving the interests of all individual Canadians. The government
January 30, 1975

said during that election campaign that if re-elected it would reintroduce the May 6 budget. The new budget does carry forward the proposals of that earlier one, together with additional measures aimed at meeting the economic circumstances we are presently facing. But the government must be alert to any signs of increasing weakness in the Canadian economy. It must be ready to move quickly and to go even further than proposed in this budget by way of fiscal policy measures but also through monetary policy, direct employment measures and other programs to help counteract any further decline in our economy.
To conclude, I want to say, as I did when speaking about the bill to implement the changes in the sales tax proposed in the new budget, that on balance I believe the measure before us today should have the support of parliament and the Canadian people.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak on Bill C-49 dealing with the changes brought in by the November budget, most of which were held over from the May budget. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) stated on Tuesday in the House that he had the essential objective of the budget in mind, to deal simultaneously with the twin problems of inflation and slower growth. He maintains that it is aimed at stimulating increased output and productive capacity in order to lessen inflationary pressures and to maintain economic performance. He mentioned that he would stem erosion in the value of savings. The government has paid little attention to people who have saved money. I must say that from a very practical point of view, those who are over 50 years of age and saving money in pension plans would do better to buy things now and to go into retirement not with money in the bank but with tangible assets.
The budget has not taken into account the very severe recession that has occurred in the United States and in western Europe, where massive attempts are being made to stimulate their economies. Many knowledgeable economists now foresee that business will improve in the next nine months or so, but it is very likely to be followed by what some people forecast to be severe inflation which will make what we have just gone through seem like a mild shower. It is generally recognized that the enormous amounts of money available and the spending by the three levels of government, mainly federal and provincial, are the main inflationary factors in our economy, factors which we as legislators can do something about. The minister himself, in a speech to the Canadian Club of Toronto on Monday, May 27, on page 13 of his speech said:
-I move to inject additional stimulus into the economy in the least inflationary way by cutting taxes rather than by increasing government spending.
The minister himself has agreed that government spending has become so great that it has lost its traditional stance, which is to stimulate growth by government spending. We know that the minister himself agreed that further government expenditures are likely to reduce growth. The minister in his budget forecast that in 1976 government expenditures will have increased 95 per cent,
Income Tax
in a four-year period, to $28.8 billion. In view of the enormous increase in revenue earned from income tax, one appreciates the great reluctance of the government to cut this to a realistic level. The minister must realize that when stating that he was giving a 15 per cent income tax cut, he was by no means offsetting the inflation factor which governments love so dearly and in which they have a vested interest because of the enormous tax revenues produced so easily and so simply.
A taxpayer, in considering the tax cuts of the government, can only say that the government's tax cut is a fraction of the effect of inflation on his income. He cannot help being cynical as the government condescendingly refrains from taking quite as much as it could, making no allowance for inflation, and he knows in fact that his real tax liability, his personal income tax, is still relatively greater than it was before.
Madam Speaker, I think that this is the time for the government to make some further judicious cuts in income tax without being accused of overstimulating the economy. Even the minister himself has stated that excess government spending is one of the main factors fueling inflation in our modern economy. Why not allow the individual citizens who work to have some more of their hard earned dollars, particularly those in the lower and middle-income groups? Some will spend it, it is true, but I think they will spend it more wisely than the government would, and more productively.
We have seen the automobile, the electronics industry and, of course, the housing industry hard hit by the recession. More money in the hands of the consumer should help to stimulate some of these durable goods sectors and give more balance to the economy. Some of the money would go, I am sure, into an area that has long been forgotten, an area which is terribly important, in my opinion, and has not received the attention that is necessary both from professional economists and from government spenders; that is, the rewards of savings. Madam Speaker, savings eventually depend on the outlook of the individual concerned. Years ago people saved for their retirement, for their hospital bills, and so on. These things have now been taken care of, and with the advent of increased old age security and the maturing of the Canada Pension Plan, enforced savings through taxation has much reduced the need to save.
Because of spiralling inflation, many people are now becoming sadly disillusioned with their registered retirement funds and with their pensions. There are substantial reasons why at this time the government could give a further modest tax reduction. Government balances are at a comfortable $5 billion, $2.5 billion more than a year ago, due to the Canada Savings Bonds campaign. Tax revenues are running well ahead of projections. There is ample room here for a judicious tax reduction, but this govern-

January 30, 1975
Income Tax
ment believes that it knows better than the individual how his money should be spent. The imposition of the surcharge on existing tax levels for most businesses, and increases for the resource industries will have the effect, for business generally, of cutting back on the capital spending on which this government is counting to make the economy move this year.
Madam Speaker, the question of savings will become more important as time goes on. There are enormous borrowings in capital investment funds to be made if Canada is to move forward and provide for its people a continuing increase in the standard of living. Even if the best economic conditions that are hoped for happen in the world generally, Canadians face, externally, some unpleasant possibilities. The Minister of Finance is quoted as saying last night in Montreal that the external payments deficit next year is expected to be $4 billion. When this is compared to the United States forecast of $20 billion, it shows how important is this aspect of our economy.
It is likely that for the year 1975, the Canadian economic performance as a whole will be clearly inadequate in the three main criteria of full employment, reasonable price stability and adequate economic growth. Inflation is certainly forecast to remain high, perhaps 11 per cent. The growth rate predicted by many economists is expected to be considerably less than 4 per cent, and more like 2.6 per cent. There will almost certainly be a reduction in the real exports performance, and the real residential construction decline is serious. There are a good many possibilities of reduced exports in the coming year that could be helped by prudent government action. For instance, in the matter of grain exports our main Canadian export of food into the markets of the world, and, incidentally, almost half of the total exports of continental North America, is in a precarious position.
Repeated strikes and interference with the movement of grain into export positions have been occurring with depressing regularity. These are likely to continue all through this coming year. We have already been told that we have lost a good deal of the Japanese rapeseed market. An officer of the Wheat Board has stated that it would require the greatest good luck and good management to export even our modest crop. The weather last fall contributed to what was considered by many to be the lowest quality crop ever produced in the west. It is perhaps fortunate that the world at large so badly needs grain that it is still saleable.
We have to remember that in the last couple of days the Wheat Board dropped the selling price of wheat by a dollar and that the Russians have cancelled many contracts with the United States. All this might indicate that the world grain shortage has eased. Weaknesses are showing up. The poorer countries and the marginal countries are finding the cost of oil so expensive that there is reluctance, and perhaps inability, to buy in quantities that we are used to. Holding over export markets for grain is the doubtful ability of Canada to remain a reliable deliverer of grain and, of course, there is the huge potential of the

United States. Had the United States had a good crop year, it would have been a much tougher year for the Canadian grain producer.
Madam Speaker, the ability of the manufacturing sector of the country to sell has always been limited. We, as Canadians, have always been told that we are not to be hewers of wood and drawers of water. We are supposed to export manufactured goods. The export of manufactured goods grows increasingly clouded when you consider that the United States is now in recession and, basically, that country is the only country that can take our high-priced manufactured goods in quantity. If the confrontation between the two governments continues, our exports are in doubt.
Turning to the resource industries, they have been one of the mainstays of our Canadian economy. Our standard of living and our ability to maintain economic impetus are in the main due to our primary industries and our resource industries. They have been since the beginning of our nation, and I see no real evidence that this will change. The fight between our provinces and the federal government over the taxation of resources can be likened to two owners fighting over a horse; they fought so long that the horse died from lack of feed. A dead horse does not produce much, and that is pretty well what the resource industries have been brought to by this bitter feud.
Madam Speaker, it is no accident that the minister devoted most of his time to defending the federal government's action on the resource question. There is no doubt that this dispute has fractured Canadian unity as no other issue since the language debate. The actions of this administration have made Canadians realize that they have in Ottawa a government that is prepared to go to any lengths to club them into submission. The minister devoted much of his time to arguing that in the matter of resource taxation it was only a question of dollars. But he and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), whom he represents, made little effort to reach any accommodation with the western provinces.
It is no secret to any western Canadian that had the oil and gas resided in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, none of this violent confrontation would have taken place. There would have been long, extended consultations, with the federal government taking much less than it did from the western provinces. The province of Quebec alone is now acting as a separate state in dealing with a foreign government in the matter of uranium. The premier of the province described the federal government as merely a gate-keeper and there has been no violent reaction from this government to that statement.
Under the British North America Act the provinces were given control of their natural resources. Had this not been given, I am sure it would have been much more difficult to have kept this country together. Until recently, however, resources were not worth a great deal and we had to give incentives to develop them. As we learned in the discussion of the white paper on taxation and subsequent legislation, without depletion allowances, and so on, we would
January 30, 1975

not have developed the oil fields. Whether we should have given these allowances is debatable, but without them we certainly would have been more dependent on the world for our oil and energy.
We may quarrel with whether we took the right course, but it is the one we took. When resource prices rose sharply, the federal government and the provinces rushed in for the spoils. Who needed the money most? I suggest the provinces had first call, because in the last 30 years there has been unbroken erosion of much of the taxing power of the provinces and they have had foisted upon them enormously costly programs in health, welfare and education.
