speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I did not propose to become too involved in this debate because I had occasion to speak on December 19 when the opposition House leader brought before this
Public Service
House a very significant private member's bill respecting the right of the public to information respecting public business. The motion was that the bill be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. There was considerable debate. Although the matter before us is somewhat different in degree, it still hits upon the same topic, namely, the right of the public to acquire public information.
I was very impressed with the government at that time, something I am not too prone to say. However, they thought there was so much merit in the hon. member's suggestion and the points he made in debate that they looked upon the matter with great favour. I was impressed with the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Reid) who indicated on behalf of the government that this was a very good idea. They felt it was now time to reverse the practice that had existed up to that time.
Bill C-225 respected the right of the public to information concerning public business. This motion reads:
That an order of the House do issue for a copy of studies prepared for the Advisory Group on Executive Compensation in the Public Service comparing salaries paid to senior public servants and salaries paid to senior executives in private industry.
Is there anything confidential about that? Is there something about that motion that can be called offensive? Is it against the public interest that this order do not issue in favour of the hon. member? I really cannot see it. All that this motion, and the bill brought forward by my House leader, is trying to do is reverse the practice that exists, that is, that no information is given by the government unless it sees fit to do so. Whenever we ask for the production of papers or for information, the government, at its option, indicates that it is not in the public interest. I have been here since 1968 and have very seldom seen them do anything other than that. This not only frustrates members but the countless thousands of people whom we represent. Because this information is garnered with the tax dollar, the public should have a right to it.
This government has talked about participatory democracy. How can you have participatory democracy without allowing those who are interested in what is going on here information which is so vital to them? I know there are matters which cannot be divulged. My House leader raised the same concern in his bill. I wish to read some of the matters he believes are of a privileged nature. I will quote from Bill C-225. The hon. member recognized that there are privileges and confidentialities that must be respected. He stated with regard to this right we should always have uppermost in our minds the fact that certain information will not be divulged. He lists these in clause 4. They are any matters-
(a)	touching or concerning the security of Canada;
(b)	where any statutory or other law provides that such record or part thereof shall not be made public;
(c)	made in the course of an investigation or inquiry in the administration of the law or in the course of obtaining or giving legal advice or in contemplation of a legal proceeding;
(d)	where the information on record is elsewhere provided or available or, in the direction of any public official, may be made available under any statutory or other law;

January 30, 1975
Public Service
(e)	where the information on record is so trivial in public interest that the cost to provide or to make the record available is not in the public interest;
(f)	where the application therefor is made for a frivolous or vexatious purpose-
I know we can be charged with being guilty in this regard many times, but I hope hon. members believe that when we seek information we do it in all sincerity. Some of us will take advantage; there is no question about that.

I heard somebody, Madam Speaker, but I did not catch what he said. I want to give that member an opportunity to say it again. I guess it was a facetious remark because I am trying to make a responsible and sensible speech. Surely I have not said anything that would raise the ire of the hon. member to such an extent that it would make him interject during such a brilliant presentation. I again quote:
(g)	where the information on record is of a confidential nature exchanged by public officials within the government or between public officials of the government and any other government and is expressed to be confidential; or
(h)	where the information on record relates to the private affairs of any person or organization and, upon a balance of convenience between private and public interest, it is not in the public interest to provide or to make the record available.
When looking at all those exceptions I ask the hon. member who interjected whether we on this side have a point. All the hon. member's motion does is seek information about a comparison of salaries between senior public servants and senior executives in private industry. Surely that is not the most difficult thing to find. It was readily available when the government made this study, for what reason I do not know. However, what is important is that a study was made and the information was acquired at public expense. Other countries, and I refer to Sweden, believe the public has a right to such information unless it comes under prescribed exceptions. This is what we are hoping for. I understand that a document has already been tabled having to do with the production of information of this kind, but we on this side find it is far from satisfactory in meeting the need to which we are calling attention.
In passing, I find it strange that hon. members on the other side should be so reluctant to take part in this debate by advancing arguments similar to those they used in connection with Bill C-225. After all, are we not discussing the same thing? Bill C-225 was concerned with public information and this afternoon we are talking about documents. The two subjects are interrelated. If hon. members would refer to Hansard of Thursday, December 19, they would find that in the closing minutes of the debate the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, who was speaking on behalf of the government, indicated that those of us who supported the bill had made such an excellent case that he would move a motion along the lines that the bill be withdrawn and the subject matter referred to the joint committee on statutory instruments.
Well, Madam Speaker, if that was the attitude taken by members on the other side toward Bill C-225, why the

hesitation now with respect to motion No. 3. on the order paper? Why the inconsistency? We might as well consider the whole subject at one time and refer it to the standing committee. I do not understand the hesitation of hon. members opposite. I hope someone will get up over there and say, "The hon. member has a point. We agreed to it in connection with Bill C-225; it is therefore incumbent upon us to take similar action today and see that the matter is referred to the appropriation standing committee." In this case, of course, it is the committee on statutory instruments.
Every now and then, in any event, there is bound to be a difference of opinion between the public and the departments or agencies of government as to whether a decision to withhold information is taken within the accepted rules-if we ever get satisfactory rules. Under the rules which currently apply, no one can challenge a government decision. If the government says that certain information is on the excepted list, we are in trouble because there is no provision for appeal. This is a matter in which the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) should show some interest. I do not think he is particularly concerned about it, though he ought to be. He wants to reform parliamentary procedure and he should show some readiness to meet the needs of the public.
During the debate to which I have referred, my hon. friend from Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) said that when such a difference of opinion arose the question should be referred to a court-to a judge-for settlement. If hon. members wish, I can quote the relevant passage from Hansard; I have it before me. On the other hand, if they appreciate the point I am making, there is no need for me to refer to the particular passage. All we are contending is that there should be provision for appeal to another tribunal when there is a difference about the interpretation of the rules. The new arrangements would apply to whatever government was in office-not only to a Liberal government but to a Conservative government or one of any other complexion. I do not think this demand is an unreasonable one. Participation in governmental affairs means a lot to the survival of our country. I think we have gone too far in the direction of leaving out of discussion the people we represent.
Politicians are in trouble everywhere today because we do not keep our ears to the ground. The move I am suggesting would be a step in the right direction; it would show that we are responsive to public opinion. The public has great difficulty in understanding what we are doing. In particular, the public does not know what the government is doing. There are questions on the order paper which have great great importance to the public.
I shall not belabour the point. I commend the hon. member who brought this motion forward for discussion. If it is not accepted today, we intend to bring it back again anyway. In conclusion, I wish the parliamentary secretary were here so that he might have the opportunity of repeating his contribution to the debate on Bill C-225. On that occasion, members on the other side accepted what the hon. member for Peace River had to say. Why do they not accept the argument today? I see many members across the aisle following this discussion intently. Hopefully, they will take the same position today as they did
January 30, 1975

with regard to the bill put forward in December, at which time they agreed that the subject matter should be referred to the standing committee for consideration.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to make a few remarks in connection with this motion. I listened carefully to the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander). He made a number of good points, but I do not think the motion itself is acceptable. On October 1, 1974, the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) asked-
That an order of the House do issue for a copy of studies prepared for the Advisory Group on Executive Compensation in the Public Service comparing salaries paid to senior public servants and salaries paid to senior executives in private industry.
This was really a notice of motion for the production of papers. An answer was submitted as follows:
The studies prepared for the Advisory Group on Executive Compensation in the Public Service contained salary data taken from several surveys concerning the movement of executive salaries both within and outside the federal public service. Data taken from these surveys is considered to be proprietary.
On these grounds, the information was not provided. This answer appeared not to have satisfied the hon. member, hence the debate on the subject which followed. Hopefully, some additional information has been provided during this debate, and I am sure that more information can be provided to the hon. member through questions put on the order paper.
I think it is important, Madam Speaker, to note that there are many reasons why studies prepared for the Advisory Group on Executive Compensation in the Public Service should be exempt from production. As a result of the debate in 1973 on the question of the production of papers, the government at that time, through the House leader, set forth the general principles guiding the government in its policy on the production of papers. I think it is agreed that the papers requested in the motion now under discussion fall under several items, (e), (q) and (s), and should be exempted from production for those reasons, namely, that they are papers containing information, the release of which could allow or result in direct personal financial gain or loss by a person or a group of persons; that they are papers that are private or confidential and not of public or official character, or that the papers requested were submitted or received in confidence by the government from sources outside the government.
Making public the confidential information requested by the government of the private sector would create a lack of confidence in government. Further requests for such confidential data would not be heeded. For example, the information deposited with the pay research bureau is confidential. If it were made public, in future such data would become unobtainable, which in turn would have a serious impact on the collective bargaining process in the public service.
Although the advisory group has not provided quantitative comparisons of salary rates in the public service and other sectors of the economy in their reports to the gov-
Public Service
ernment, the group has made qualitative statements concerning the relationship of executive salaries in the public service and other sectors of the economy, and enunciated and made recommendations on the policies that would govern their recommendations for the revision of public service senior executive salary ranges, and these should be sufficient information. In its first report of December 2, 1968, the advisory group concluded that existing rates of pay for senior executives were too low. Executive rates of pay had not been maintained reasonably in line with those paid for comparable duties and responsibilities in the economy at large.
They did not mean to suggest, however-and I quote- "that the rates of pay for executive personnel in the public service should be fixed on the basis of some mechanical equation with those applying to executive personnel in particular institutions in the private sector of the economy without regard to the important differences that exist in other conditions of employment, including security of tenure. We do not believe, however, that the continued efficiency and effectiveness of the public service, which are of great importance to both the government and the tax paying public, depend in some significant degree on the maintenance of reasonably competitive rates of pay for senior public servants".
In preparing its third report dated May 15, 1973, tabled in the House of Commons October 5, 1973, the advisory group examined the trend in executive salary movement outside the public service and noted that these showed a greater increase than executive salaries in the government. During the years 1970, 1971 and 1972, for example, executive salaries outside the federal public service increased by an average of 21.7 per cent, compared with 13.8 per cent for public service executives. The advisory group considered, as well, the movement of negotiated salary settlements within the various groups in the public service and noted that these also exceeded the rate of increase in executive salaries. They concluded that the then existing executive salary framework must be revised. Their recommended salary structure was implemented in two stages effective January 1, 1973 and April 1, 1974. The current salary structure for senior executives is that recommended by the advisory group in its third report, with the general $500 increase awarded to public servants on April 1, 1974, added to the senior executive officer salary ranges only, and not to those of deputy ministers.
In these two years since the last advisory group report, senior executive salary ranges increased by 7.8 per cent in 1973 for the 15 months January 1, 1973, to April 1, 1974, and 8.8 per cent in 1974, for a compounded total of 17.3 per cent. During the same two years the size of negotiated increases of major collective agreements concluded under all provincial labour jurisdictions combined was an average annual compound rate of increase of 9.8 per cent in 1973 and 12 per cent for the first six months of 1974, a compounded total of 23 per cent. These statistics were compiled by the Department of Labour.
Obviously, in the past two years public service senior executive salary ranges have not increased at as fast a pace as those established by the average negotiated collective agreement. There is nothing automatic about

January 30, 1975
Public Service
salary increases for senior executives. These are provided purely in relation to individual performance, and movement into the new salary ranges provided by the government must be consistent with satisfactory performance. In its third report the advisory group noted that senior executive salary increases had shown a clear tendency to be lower than increases in the salary ranges in the previous two years; this condition has been evident during 1973 and 1974 as well.
In summation, may I say that the Advisory Group on Executive Compensation utilizes data taken from a number of surveys such as those conducted by the American Management Association, H. V. Chapman, Hay and Associates, and the pay research bureau. These surveys provided by Hay and Associates and the pay research bureau are made available to the advisory group on the condition that the contents are not made public, and in fact are reviewed only by those people directly involved in the compensation function. If this information were to be made public, either willingly or unwillingly, the advisory group, and indeed the government, would be denied access to the information in the future. Such a breach of confidence would impair communications with not only the surveying organizations but other elements of the private sector to the extent that the acquisition of data for the purposes of maintaining comparability would be most difficult if not impossible.
To understand the need for the restricted disclosure of salary data one must be knowledgeable of the dimensions of the surveying process. First of all, salaries in the private sector, particularly at the executive level, are extremely confidential and are treated so within their own organizations as well as outside. Secondly, many employers are very reluctant, therefore, to divulge their executive salaries and do so only with the guarantee that the information will only be made available to a restricted group of participating organizations, and then only with the commitment that the information will be carefully guarded. Thirdly, the collection and distribution of salary data constitutes a significant portion of the business of the named organizations. The confidential treatment of this data is a significant characteristic of this business. If the confidence were to be breached, their business would be jeopardized.
These employers make the data available through a third party, that is, the surveying organizations, only in the knowledge that they will receive data on the salaries paid by other companies. Furthermore, I am advised that two of the surveys, being very large and very general in nature, are available to the public. I am sure that most of the information the hon. member requires could be obtained from them. As a result of the foregoing I feel the papers should not be produced, and that access to them should be denied.

Those were gloomy years and I would not want to refer now to the Diefenbaker years. The country suffered enough during those years without going back to them and referring to them unduly.
In spite of the interruption I think it is necessary to review some of the important authorities that surround this matter. I was particularly interested to note that the President of the Privy Council then quoted from Benjamin Disraeli. Certain hon. members might disallow Disraeli, and I am sure he would disallow them now as well. In any event this distinguished British statesman saw fit to express himself on this subject. As one of the great debaters in parliamentary history he had great eloquence and skill, and his words are no less true today than they were at that time. Perhaps I might just read for a moment some of the words of Disraeli:
The system of laying upon the table of the House reports from officers addressed to particular departments of the executive government is most objectionable. And the House ought not to insist upon the production of papers and correspondence which concerned the preparation and preliminary consideration of measures; they would thereby put a stop to that freedom of criticism which was always invited on such occasions, and which contributed so much to the perfection of public measures.
If the House were to insist upon the production of such documents, instead of the government getting what we get now, confidential reports, containing the most minute details of the opinions of officers, given frankly and freely, for the heads of departments, we shall have a system of reports framed for laying upon the table of the House of Commons, and those will be accompanied by "confidential reports for the head of the department alone". There have been cases in which reports of a confidential character from officers of the government have been laid upon the table of the House, to prepare the public mind and also that of Parliament, to consent to some large measure, or perhaps some considerable vote of public money; but, generally, I think it is a course which the House ought not to sanction.
My hon. friend has already cited the guidelines laid before the House by the former President of the Privy Council. These were generally acknowledged in the House to be effective and cogent reasons.

I have heard a good deal of nonsense in this Chamber in the years I have been here, but I have never heard such nonsense as I heard from the hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore (Mr. Robinson) when he spoke a few moments ago.
When speaking on this matter a week ago I did not say that public civil servants were being paid too much. I do

not ask now, nor did I at that time, for information as to salaries paid by individual corporations, the private sector of the economy, or by individual municipal and provincial governments or universities. What I did suggest, and I would reiterate today, is that we pay substantial salaries to a large number of civil servants. When I spoke last week I thought there were 850, but I now find there is a group perhaps much greater than that. The only person who would know is the President of the Treasury Board. These are civil servants who apparently are paid as members of the SX category. These are a group who are classed as the senior management complement. We do not know about those. They are hidden somewhere. That is the kind of information that we need to have.
What I said, Madam Speaker, is very simple. I said that we want to know, and I think we have a right to know, how the salaries of the senior public servants compare in broad category with salaries paid to senior executives in private industry, in provincial and municipal governments, and in organizations such as universities. I am not saying we need to know individual salaries, but there is no reason why information such as I have asked for cannot be given, not to me but to the public of Canada as a whole.
It is not surprising that the public get upset when they read about the large increases which are proposed for various groups at the same time as the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) is saying that it will be tough going for people who work at the Mint, people who work at the Post Office, and other categories of people who are making relatively low wages and salaries.
I say that the public have a right to have this kind of information in the widest possible manner, and that does not mean in the manner in which the President of the Treasury Board chooses but in a manner which may be worked out co-operatively between all members of parliament. If hon. members on the other side would stop thinking it is their private preserve, that somehow they have been anointed and will always be in government, and if they realize that the information we want is information which should be available to all the public, then this matter could be worked out quite amicably.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to take a few moments of the time of the House to address myself to one small but important aspect of the budget, one with which I disagree. I refer to the proposal that the normal land carrying costs of someone holding land for business purposes not be deductible from business income. This clause affects land speculators. I want to make a suggestion about the way in which we can, through the budget, deal with land speculators. This clause also affects the housing industry. In my submission, it affects housing for the worse. It will have the effect of slowing down supply of serviced lots and tend to increase their price.
When I talk about the development and housing industry, I am talking about an industry about which I know a great deal. Wheh I was in the practice of law I acted for land developers and people in the housing industry.
And speculators.

And I suppose for speculators. I want to make it clear that I discontinued my legal practice when I was elected. I also want to put on record,-as all of my constituents are aware because of the fact it was raised during the election campaign-that I have relatives in the housing industry. Having said that, I would also like to add that I know thousands and thousands of people in my constituency who face a very real crisis in not being able to find the kind of housing they want, and in finding that the cost of housing they have, particularly rental housing, is tending to go up and up. I am looking at the proposal the government has put before us in the total perspective of these things that I know.
In dealing with the housing industry I think that we, as a government, are entitled to use a stick and carrot approach. We ought to be encouraging, and we ought also to be tough. For example, I am an advocate of rent controls. On a temporary basis and in a situation where supply is very, very short, rent controls would be a way of keeping the lid on while new housing is created.
It is not the place in this budget debate to elaborate on rent controls, but hon. members may be interested to know that I was in Montreal this morning getting some ideas from officials who deal with rent controls in that province. They are convinced that if housing controls
January 30, 1975

were removed tomorrow, rentals would increase across the board in the province of Quebec by 45 per cent. I do not want to be simplistic in looking at that, but that means, if they are right, that rent controls in Quebec today have the effect of keeping rents 45 per cent below what they would be otherwise. That is a very interesting policy which can produce an effect like that. I urge this government and the provincial government of Ontario to look at it.
On the question of land carrying costs I feel the government is on the wrong track with the policy it has put forward. The theory is that the industry is willfully holding back land and not selling it in order to increase the price. This may well be the case with speculators, and I have no objection to these budget measures being applied to speculators to put pressure on them to turn their land over, putting it back where it can be used by people who intend to develop it for housing and other purposes.
The government of Ontario recently introduced a tax against land speculators. From what I can see, it was a very effective initiative. It had the effect of taking quite a lot of the heat off the land development industry in Ontario.
From my experience in the industry my conclusion is that the bottleneck of getting land onto the market as serviced lost is not at the level of the developer. In fact the efforts of the typical company in the business is to try to put land on to the market as serviced lots as quickly as possible. Their business is turnover, not holding back. In case after case they are the ones who take the initiative in getting an area going, in getting a plan approved, in getting agreement for services and proper zoning. The bottleneck is the approval procedure which requires reference to literally dozens of agencies, municipal, supermunicipal, provincial and so on. It is true this approval procedure has a purpose. I do not deny that the community interest has certainly to be reflected, but the bottleneck could be reduced by streamlining the required procedures so as to shorten the period between the time land is acquired and the time it is marketed as lots.
In the last few months the Province of Ontario has announced its intention to address itself to this prevalence of red tape. This indicates to me that the province itself recognizes that the bureaucratic procedures to which I have referred are in a large measure responsible for the long delays in making lots available.
Since it takes years for housing development to proceed it is obvious that the industry must have some inventory of land with which to work. If the government proposal is adopted the housing industry will be the only industry in Canada, as far as I know, whose inventory costs are not deductible. This will be damaging to the industry just as it would be to other businesses if this principle were applied. We are looking to the industry to produce housing and deal with what may be the number one priority in Canada, yet we are doing things which will damage it and reduce its capacity.
What will be the effects of this policy? First, if the cost of holding land and bringing serviced land to market goes up, the industry will obviously try to pass on the extra
Income Tax
cost to its customers, and in a market like housing, where there is tremendous shortage of supply, I believe the industry is likely to succeed in doing so. The result will be higher-priced lots.
Second, this policy would mean that more capital will be required to enable a company to stay in business. If a company is not getting the deduction, if it has to pay more by way of taxes, additional capital is needed in order to carry on the business. This is bound to lead to increased concentration within the industry; smaller firms will have to do less or drop out all together, and the larger firms, many of which are foreign-owned, will be able to move in, thus reducing competition. To my mind this is an undesirable consequence, yet it is a probable consequence of the measure contained in the budget.
Third, I believe it will lead to an inventory reduction on the part of companies in the industry. If they cannot carry their inventories they will have to sell part of them. I concede that selling land in this way would tend to reduce prices. But what land will the companies be selling? Obviously it would be the land which is relatively remote from the urban areas, not the land which is closest to being sold as serviced land. What will happen is this: the land sold will drop outside the planning process and less attention will be paid to bringing it into use. It is also fairly likely that the remaining inventory a company holds will increase in value, the consequence of which would be to increase its cost. Surely this is not the way to contribute to an increase in housing.
In summary, this proposed policy should be re-thought by the government. It would be easy to introduce proposals which would apply only to land speculators, to those in the industry who do not develop their land, who do not provide serviced lots, who do not provide housing. This kind of distinction is already drawn in the Income Tax Act for another purpose. I am asking that this distinction should be applied in this field. The government should not take the steps it proposes here, steps which will damage the very industry to which we are looking to resolve what is possibly Canada's most serious problem- the shortage of housing and its high cost. The bottleneck is not the industry. The bottleneck is government.

The
bill before us, Bill C-49, is a bill to amend the law relating to income tax and to implement the many changes in personal and corporate income tax proposed in the budget of November 18.
When the hon. member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray) was lauding the United States food stamp program I was interested in the fact that he drove the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) over to the opposition side for a few minutes.
I wanted to hear what it sounded like over there.

The essential purpose of the budget is to deal simultaneously with the twin problems of inflation and slower growth. However, one of our main difficulties is that in the minds of a broad section of the public there are now no more opportunities left to do so. I listened carefully to the Minister of

January 30, 1975
Income Tax
Finance (Mr. Turner) defending his position as he spoke in general terms of the measures in the budget which affect the resource industries. I am, of course, particularly concerned about the status of the resource industries of western Canada and the effect the government's policies, or lack of policies, is likely to have on my own area. I shall say more about this later on.
I consider the bill before us to be the most important bill to have arisen so far from the budget speech. It is lengthy and complicated, extending over almost 300 pages. Many of the proposed amendments are technical in nature, but there are some important aspects of this legislation which should be fully debated. One thing of which we can be sure is that the tax forms resulting from Bill C-49 will be even more complicated than in the past. There will certainly be more civil servants appointed to look after us; the number of people employed by the Department of National Revenue rose by some 1,200 last year alone to more than 20,000, and this number is like'y to be increased even further.
Clause 42 provides for the deferring of income tax in connection with grain delivered in one year and paid for in the following year. I notice the draftsmen have been very careful to insert the words "without interest". I cannot understand why a producer who sells his grain in September, for instance, and does not receive payment until the next calendar year, cannot receive interest on the money.
Clause 30 has to do with the deduction of $1,000 with respect to contributions under a registered home ownership savings plan. Again, I cannot for the life of me understand why producers cannot be given the same sort of deal in respect of farms or ranches. In the area I represent Farm Credit Corporation loans now average $50,000. Within a couple of years it will be very close to an average of $100,000. It seems only reasonable in the case of an agricultural producer whose farm is his real retirement plan that he should be allowed to take several thousand dollars before tax and put the money into his operation.
The registered home ownership plan creates several interesting problems. One is that you cannot contribute to the plan in the year you buy the house. Consequently, a person who takes advantage in 1975 of his $1,000 exemption cannot use the funds to buy a house before 1976, which is clearly not much use in helping to curb the falling home construction market this year. It appears that it is possible for both husband and wife to contribute $1,000 each a year, up to $20,000. It also appears that if the home is in only one spouse's name, the other spouse can take advantage of the plan, accumulate up to $10,000, and then, I suppose, use the money later on to furnish the home of his or her spouse.
As the hon. member for York Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) said in his speech, it is, of course, through income tax legislation that the government receives most of its revenue, revenue that it always spends. Also as he said, I believe that to the extent this revenue is lessened, government expenditures are lessened. Control the government's revenue and you control its spending habits. Conversely,

when excessive revenues accrue to the government, they encourage future excess spending by the government.
It is our duty as an opposition to ensure that this government handles public funds responsibly and prudently. Thus, it is fair to ask whether the government's revenue forecasts are reasonable, has there been proper planning, etc.? I also believe, most important of all, we should ask whether ministers know where they are going and do we, as a country, know where we are going?
The $1,000 interest exemption provision has an unfortunate twist in that a farmer, for example, who for business purposes borrows money and pays interest, would have to deduct this interest from any other interest income earned before claiming the credit. As a result many businessmen or farmers will find that the provision is not available to them. It seems to me that the primary producers very seldom get a break.
The minister mentioned many special factors accounting for our problems in Canada, but they do not account for all of our problems and for all our inflation. For a good number of years now our economy has had a serious underlying bias toward inflation, and I believe that the roots of that bias lie chiefly in the rising aspirations of people everywhere. We seem to be in a hurry for more and more of what we consider the good things of life, and I do not question that because, properly directed, this can be s powerful force for our betterment.
Our difficulties arise, however, when people in general seek to reach their goals by means of short cuts, and this is what has been happening in Canada. Our people have been encouraged to take short cuts by the actions of this government. Of late, the government has encouraged individuals to depend less and less on their own initiative and more and more upon government in order to achieve their economic objectives.
Nowadays the public expects the government to maintain prosperous economic conditions, to limit such declines in employment as may occasionally occur, to ease the burden of job loss through illness or retirement, and to sustain the incomes of just about everybody. Unfortunately, in the process of doing so we have seen the government's budget go completely out of control. Wages and prices have become less responsive to market forces, and inflation has emerged as the most dangerous economic ailment of our time. Our businesses, small and large, have seen their costs soar with increasing wage rates and sharply rising prices for materials. Accountants reckon the value of inventories-machinery and equipment used in production-at original cost rather than at current inflated prices, and this practice has created an illusory element in profits, an element that is just not available for distribution or for replacing the inventories and equipment at appreciably higher prices. But, worst of all, this illusory part of the profits is subject to income tax, thus aggravating the deterioration of real business profits.
I think that tax accounting in regard to inventories and depreciation allowances for business is unfair under the present act. A more equitable plan is needed to allow for inflation. We are now at a stage where the distortions and injustices brought about by inflation have contributed materially to the distrust of government officials and of
January 30, 1975

government policies, and even to some loss of confidence in our brand of society.
I think that this can be very well illustrated by the quarrel that took place between Ottawa and the western provinces over petroleum revenues. I can sum up the feeling quite simply by saying that the provinces wanted that money for long-term industrial development, including the development of future gas and oil supplies. They feared, and I feel rightly so, that Ottawa wanted the money for short-term welfare-massive handouts to mounting numbers of unemployed. They feel there will be nothing to show for this welfare spending, spending which not only is totally non-productive but, indeed, counter-productive, though it may help the government buy some public order.
In his speech the Minister of Finance repeatedly argued the right of all Canadians to share in the benefits of the natural resources of this country. We have no argument with that; it is the manner of operation of this government that is unsettling to us.
I think it is worth while looking back a few years. In the second world war we were completely dependent upon the United States for petroleum. We should never forget that the United States government's oil policy treated Canada as if it were another state of the union. They were our great and good friends in those days. Leduc did not become operative until February, 1947. In 1961 Canada's national oil policy reserved the markets west of the Ottawa Valley to western Canadian crude. It freed the markets east to buy at their choice. They imported foreign crude, all for a saving of one and one-quarter cents a gallon at the pump. The cost to Canada in royalties, employment, etc., was $1 billion, according to a 1965 study by Dr. D. E. Armstrong of McGill University.
Repeated attempts to stop this drain on our economy by a pipe line to Montreal were rebuffed. Our balance of payments suffered as imports of foreign crude increased in the Montreal refineries. The government would not force a cent a gallon on the east to help the western oil industry. Even the Department of National Defence supplied the air base at Trenton from Montreal.
In 1967, during the Arab-Israeli war, the flow of foreign oil to Montreal was reduced. We were in a rather tight spot but were saved by the United States, which used its own domestic production to supply us. Now that country, whose generosity saved Montreal in 1967, is to be penalized; exports to the United States are to be cut off altogether.
This government's policies appear to be a deliberate attempt to destroy a necessary Canadian industry. In 1970 the federal government revoked, without prior consultation or notice, federal oil and gas land orders of 1961. For four years the petroleum industry was left without any basis for establishing the royalties and terms under which half of the exploratory permits of the Arctic operated, so most of the activity is confined to commitments made years ago. Now we have double royalty rates on gas and oil from the western provinces, and the Petroleum Administration Act will extend federal price control over natural gas as well as oil.
Income Tax
In my own little corner of southwest Saskatchewan the oil field service people have withdrawn their services. The oil wells are operating at a production rate of 17 per cent capacity in my area. We used to have 800 people in my area directly employed in oil field operations, but that number is now down to 200 people, and many of them will not be able to hang on for much longer. Managements of those companies out there are quietly going along with this withdrawal of services by the oil field people, because management can be fined $1,000 a day per well if they shut down, and this withdrawal of services of their employees offers a very convenient way out.
When the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) was asked if he would take some initiative with the province of Saskatchewan in trying to resolve the situation he replied only that this was a helpful suggestion. Is it any wonder that the government's record over the past four years with this industry is cause for alarm? With all the tensions we have in Canada did the Minister of Finance have to add to them with his budget? Was this an attempt to divert attention from his own mismanagement? The same can be asked in respect of the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board with his opening up of the Crowsnest Pass freight rates. This appears to be another red herring.
The last few years have seen changes in relation to the government and private sectors in Canada that none of us could have predicted. Who would have thought, even a few years ago, that we would hear a minister of the Crown suggest in this House that we nationalize the Canadian Pacific Railway, or hear another minister of the Crown within the last few months suggest that we nationalize our grain handling industry?
The western provinces have stated quite rightly that they need money from their depleting oil resources to build a broader base on which to support future generations. In my own province of Saskatchewan we only have to go back a few years to look at an agreement between the federal government and Great Britain concerning our greatest resource industry, our grain industry. We had just come through the 1930's when Saskatchewan suffered a shocking decrease in numbers of people. We lost over 250,000 people from the province of Saskatchewan. This alone should give some indication of the fears and social disillusionment created by difficulties there. Then World War II came along and, I suppose, softened us up for what was to come next.
The agreement I mentioned was known as the British Wheat Agreement and was entered into by the government of Canada. It was an undertaking on our behalf to supply 600 million bushels for four years, and was signed on July 24, 1946. To make a long story short, for the first two years the wheat was sold for $1.55 a bushel, No. 1 wheat at the Lakehead. During the third year the price was cut down 30 cents a bushel, to $1.25, and in the fourth year the basic price was down another 25 cents a bushel, to an even $1 a bushel. When this agreement was signed the world price of wheat was around $2 a bushel. You can imagine the immediate reaction of the western producers. To say it was one of surprise would be understating it. The British Minister of Food publicly stated:

Canadian farmers were selling their 1946 wheat to the United Kingdom at nearly one dollar a bushel cheaper than a price they could get in the open market.
Over the total four-year life of this agreement the estimated loss to western grain producers was upward of $700 million. We still think it was hardly fair to place the burden of Canada's generosity wholly on our grain industry. So much for the government of Canada's intervention in respect of this great renewable resource!
We know that opportunities do not arrive on a platter, but that they have to be originated by creative and imaginative minds. The personal income tax reductions proposed in Bill C-49 are inadequate considering Canada's present economic condition, and I do not think they will spark much imagination and creativity.
Let me give some figures prepared by the Institute for Policy Analysis at the University of Toronto. They show the economic outlook for 1975 as indicating that the Canadian growth in real gross national product will be marginal, probably not greater than half our capabilities; that residential construction will fall by 16 per cent; that exports will fall by 3 per cent; that inflation will remain at over 10 per cent, while unemployment will remain near 7 per cent.
In the third quarter of 1974 personal income tax revenue rose by a startling 28 per cent with no real growth in the economy. Unemployment benefits paid in 1974 amounted to over $2 billion. In the last three years the Unemployment Insurance Commission has distributed $6 billion compared to $2 billion in the previous three years. The unemployment rate, however, has averaged 5.8 per cent in the- Turner years compared to 5.7 per cent in the previous three year period.
We are all familiar with the slogan "The land is strong", and Canada with its abundance of natural resources and primary products has been able to stand the stresses and strains better than almost any other country. Canada is one of the few developed nations which benefits from the worldwide boom in food and raw material prices. However, without such resources Canada would have had a disastrous negative real growth.
I doubt that Canada will be so fortunate in the years ahead. Already we see world commodity prices falling as demand and ability to pay lessen. We will survive all right, but the price we shall have to pay is unknown.
I believe the tax reduction provisions of this bill are inadequate. I hope they will be fully explained at the committee stage. I would like to know why the Minister of Finance refuses to give a substantial tax break to the Canadian public. It is clear from his own figures that he took an unnecessary $1 billion from the Canadian public in 1974 and, as I said before, that was a year when direct personal taxes jumped a startling 27.6 per cent. The cost of operating this government is out of line with our ability to pay.
The bill before us proposes to increase the deductions in respect of personal income tax for 1975 by a mere 3 per cent. I do not believe this is adequate. It is very small relief when we realize what inflation has done to real income. This deduction should be increased by a further 5 per cent, as a minimum, amounting to some $500 million

less in federal income tax. I can assure you that this amount quite properly should be left for the hard-pressed taxpayer.
I would like to see the government take some steps to assure the taxpayer that further burdens on him will be avoided. The government has tried to give the people of Canada the idea that they can live with inflation and adjust to it rather than fight it. This is just not sound or practical. Escalator arrangements are not the answer; they weaken the discipline needed to conduct business and government affairs prudently and efficiently.
Mr. ]ohn Gilbert (Broadview): Mr. Speaker, if the people of Canada knew on July 8 what they know today about the budget proposals of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) we would now probably have a minority government, in all probability with the leader of the Conservative party as the Prime Minister of Canada.
Hear, hear!

May I say that having the leader of the Conservative party as Prime Minister would probably be far better than having the leader of the Liberal party as the Prime Minister of Canada at this time.
Back on July 8 we had all the signs of unemployment and high inflation, and on November 18 the Minister of Finance gave us his responses. Let me catalogue those responses of the Minister of Finance to high unemployment and inflation in Canada. First of all he says, as a very optimistic projection, that by 1975 we will have a real growth of 4 per cent. We must bear in mind that in 1973 we had a real growth of 7.1 per cent, and in 1974 a real growth between 4 per cent and 4] per cent. Now the pessimistic Minister of Finance is telling the people of Canada that the best they can expect in real growth is 4 per cent.
The second point is that the Minister of Finance said that in 1975 there will be 250,000 new jobs created in Canada. May I say that in 1974 we had 390,000 new jobs created.
Under the Liberals.

What a downtrend we have from 390,000 in 1974 to 250,000 in 1975. May I remind the minister that that 250,000 includes people who have retired and people who have died. They call those new jobs, and it is included in that figure of 250,000. That is the response of the Minister of Finance to unemployment.
In regard to housing starts the minister, in a very eloquent way, said that it is hoped housing starts will be approximately 198,000 in 1975. May I remind the minister that in 1973 there were 269,000 starts, and in 1974 there were 220,000 starts. Now the minister says to the people of Canada that the best that we can hope for is 198,000 housing starts this year. Under the legislation that the government is attempting to pass in Bill C-46 the best that they can hope for is 202,000.
With regard to his response to inflation the minister says that we are striving to get below the two digit level
January 30, 1975

next year. Can you imagine that, Mr. Speaker? Anything below 10 per cent, and the minister calls it a remarkable achievement for the government of Canada and his party. This is the response of the minister in his budget speech of November 18.
Then he says that he will give some income tax cuts to the upper income people and to the corporate elite, but he will give little or nothing to the low and moderate income people.
No wonder Herb Gray quit.

This is the minister's response to the income tax approach to inflation. It is abundantly clear that the government intends to rely exclusively on the private sector, and to increase the incentives to those people who operate the private sector. There is little or no government intervention in pricing and investment decisions of large corporations, or increased involvement in the resource and housing sectors. Let me give you two examples.
I am glad that the spokesman for the Conservative Party is here tonight to hear what I have to say with regard to Syncrude. All the studies have indicated that in the early 1980's there will be a serious oil shortage in Canada. What is the response? We have the Syncrude development, which is a consortium of large multinational corporations attempting to develop the Alberta tar-sands, and which have said to the government of Canada, after one of them dropped out because it was no longer financially attracted, that they need money and other concessions in order to operate, and the Minister of Finance has given them concessions which he has not given to the ordinary manufacturing industry in Canada.
He has said to the petroleum industry that the government will give tax deductions ranging from 30 per cent in 1974 to 28 per cent in 1^75, and to 25 per cent in 1976, and that the government will add to that 100 per cent write-off costs for exploration. This is the approach of the Minister of Finance, and he has also said that he will give back the first two year write-off with regard to any machinery, something which was to come to an end in 1974.
These are the three measures that the minister has given to Syncrude in the face of an oil shortage in 1980. I would have thought that a Minister of Finance with any foresight would have said that it is time that the government of Canada took an active part in the oil industry in Canada, and that the government would go it alone with the co-operation of the provinces across the country. I feel certain that if he had gone to Alberta and Ontario, and asked them to join in a joint venture with regard to the development of the Alberta oilsands, we would not have any fears, and we would not have to give the concessions to the oil companies which we are giving today. Further, we would have some assurance that in the years to come the price of oil to Canadians would be a proper and reasonable price. We have no assurance that that will happen today.
The Minister of Finance in his rare rhetorical form spoke to a group in Montreal last night, and he said that Arab oil money would be welcome in Canada for housing provided that it went to the private sector, and that it went to the provincial governments. May I remind the

minister that yesterday the spokesmen for the provincial housing agencies across the country met at the Chateau Laurier and announced that they were gravely disappointed in the approach of the government to housing, and the lack of financial help from the government in regard to housing.
This is one of the most important sectors of the economy, and we have the Minister of Finance saying no to Arab oil money, unless it is debt money and unless it is going to the provinces and to the private sector. I agree with him that it should be debt money, but surely he should call in the provinces and say that he will deal directly with the Arab countries to obtain moneys to put into housing so that we can have proper and decent housing at reasonable cost. That is what he should have said last night. But no, he put a limitation on it. He said that it has to go to the private sector and that it has to go to the provincial governments. He should have said that the federal government will do all that is reasonable to stimulate the housing industry so that Canadians can have decent and proper housing at a reasonable cost as a basic human right. That is not what the minister did.
The personal income tax deductions in Bill C-49 are regressive in their impact and tend to provide greater benefits to the high income groups and widen the disparity with the lower income groups. Let me give you an example, Mr. Speaker. Under the tax reductions of the Minister of Finance a single individual taxpayer earning $6,000 a year will save $183 as a result of the tax reductions. A single taxpayer earning $30,000 will save $651. A married man with two children under 16 years of age with an income of $6,000 will have a saving of $214. A married man with two children under the age of 16 with an income of $30,000 will save $622. It is like giving a cake to the upper income groups and crumbs to the lower and moderate income groups. That is the substance of the personal income tax reductions of the Minister of Finance, and there is absolutely nothing for people whose income is so low that tax is not payable. Mr. Speaker, it is regressive, not progressive, and it fits into the biblical quotation that "to him who hath, more shall be added; and for him who hath not, even that which he hath shall be taken away." That is the approach of the Minister of Finance with regard to the income groups across the country.
What do the personal income tax reductions do to the purchasing power of the low and moderate income people? They do nothing to strengthen their purchasing power, nothing to increase their disposable income in the light of the two digit inflation that the Minister of Finance has announced.

He spoke of the elimination of the milk subsidy. The election took place, and a few months later the government took the subsidy off milk.
Shame!

The hon. member for Windsor West spoke about the absolute rip-off which took place with regard to sugar prices in Canada. He told us of the response of the government, namely, that if it continued the government would set up a national sugar purchasing board. The hon. member for Windsor West suggested angrily that what should have happened was that the Prices Review Board should have made an immediate study and exposed the sugar companies for what they are with regard to the rip-off to which they are subjecting Canadians.
I think that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) could have stepped in and taken measures to improve the sugar beet industry across the country so that next year we do not run into the same situation. The hon. member for Windsor West summed it all up by saying that one of the difficulties he saw was the failure of the government to implement the anti-profiteering bill. We in the NDP voted against the anti-profiteering bill on the basis that it was a sham and a delusion. After the response of the Minister of Finance on November 8 I think that we would have been a little better off supporting the anti-profiteering bill.
You should have. You ran out on that bill.
I did not.
Your party ran out.

We opposed that bill because it was a sham and a delusion. I thought that the Minister of Finance and his colleagues would have treated it as such, and would not have given it the teeth and the strength that are necessary to enforce such an anti-profiteering bill. The more I hear the Minister of Finance, the more I realize that he would not have given the strength that would have been required to enforce that bill.
I have always said nice things about you, John.

Now I come to the measures that the Minister of Finance, that charming man with the rhetoric of Cicero, announced with regard to housing. This is what he said in his budget speech:
I have already referred to the short-term prospects for construction of new housing. The projected weakness in this sector of our economy troubles me a good deal. It threatens to reduce employment, raise production costs and increase housing prices and rents. Even more important, a reduction in the supply of new
housing could lead to a lower standard of accommodation than Canadians deserve.
I could not agree more with him that the budget proposals that he has announced will do the things that he feared most. When he talks about 200,000 starts in 1975, and we had 269,000 in 1973 and 220,000 in 1974, it certainly gives strength to his argument. In the response that the minister has given, he said he will reduce the sales tax on building and construction materials from 12 per cent to 5 per cent. The Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson) and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) were supposed to set up a monitoring committee to make sure that the difference in the sales tax would be passed on to the purchasers. It is a very safe wager that up to tonight no monitoring committee has been set in place for the protection of purchasers with regard to the reduction of the sales tax.
When I think of the $500 grant to first time purchasers of new houses, I find that it certainly does not apply to people who live in cities such as Toronto and Vancouver, because of the high cost of houses there and the high limits they impose with regard to that $500 grant.
When I think of the withdrawal of the earlier government request to lending institutions to limit high mortgage loans on medium and low priced housing, I find that this will enhance the profitability of the companies but do nothing to lower prices, interest rates, or rents.
One of the main items in the budget was the Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan. He said that this would provide a new source of mortgage funds. I would ask him what was the purpose of the mortgage financing mechanism bill? I thought that that bill was passed, with the support of the Conservative Party, for the purpose of setting up mortgage investment companies to attract more capital to the mortgage market. It has done nothing of that nature, and in fact when that bill was being passed I happened to be speaking to the former president of CMHC and he told me privately that the mortgage financing mechanism bill would have little or no effect. That is precisely what has happened. Now we have the Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan. In that plan there is no commitment that the institutions will direct their moneys into housing. That is a very important direction. All it does is to provide a tax haven or a shelter for the upper income groups to enjoy a handsome tax advantage. It does nothing to help the lower and moderate income people.
The other matter is that the deductibility of capital cost allowances on apartment buildings against all sources of income will attract a significant amount of private equity capital to the construction of new rental housing. That is the reason that the Minister of Finance gave with regard to this measure. It would be fair to wager that this would do nothing to reduce rents.
At the beginning of the debate this evening we heard the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan) make two points. One was that it was an advantage to have rent controls, and he recounted the experience of people in Quebec according to whom, if rent controls were taken off, there would be a 45 per cent increase in rents. He said that the government of Ontario also should impose rent controls. The NDP in British Columbia has imposed rent

January 30, 1975

controls as a temporary measure to prevent gouging by landlords.
The other point that the hon. member for York Centre made was a criticism of the government with regard to the non-deductibility of land costs. Madam Speaker, the government has not prevented the deductibility of land costs until such time as the land has been sold. The hon. member for York Centre thinks this is a serious problem with regard to housing in Ontario.
Let me remind the hon. member that in Toronto and other large cities urban land is in the control of five or six developers in each city. He need not take my word for it. In one of its reports CMHC indicated that the large tracts of land surrounding urban centres are in the hands of large developers. What the hon. member for York Centre wants is a deductibility with regard to land costs.
The Minister of Finance knows that companies like Cadillac Construction paid little or no taxes on their developments in the past. It is one of the loopholes that the minister has closed. It is about time they were denied this deductibility of land costs until such time as the land is sold. That is the one thing for which I will give the minister credit.
There are only two significant changes that I can see in the budget; one is the deductibility of $1,000 on private pensions, and the other the deductibility of $1,000 for bank or mortgage interest or dividends. This is a very insignificant step, but the minister gave such a large chunk of deductions to the upper income groups that he would not have been able to sleep at night had he not thrown a crumb to the lower an moderate income families.
The Minister of Finance is what is known as a consensus minister. He attempts to get the consensus of people across the country, and then package legislation to make it attractive to them. What he does, however, is make it attractive to the rich and the upper class, and just slightly attractive to the poor and moderate income people. To allow deductibility of $1,000 on private pensions and $1,000 for bank or bond interest is like giving a handshake to someone who is starving.
It is time we put our house in order, Madam Speaker, and put people first rather than corporations. It is time we had a tax system which implemented some of the proposals made by Mr. Carter, and it is time we had a distribution of income that did not create the disparities that now exist. If we had that as a philosophy then this would be a country in which we could be proud to live, and proud to work-
Are you not?
-rather than a country which I am proud to live in, but where I am disgusted and disappointed with the "divide and con" approach of the Liberal government.

Why is the automobile industry now asking for a corporate cut and being joined by the unions? The unions are asking for a corporate cut in taxes at this time. I should like to hear what the hon. member has to say about that.

Madam Speaker, I thank the hon. member for his question. I did not know the trade unions were asking the Minister of Finance for a corporate tax cut in order to stimulate production. If that is so, I am surprised. I would have thought the trade unions would be asking the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) to bring automobile prices in Canada down to parity with prices in the United States. I can appreciate the corporations going after the minister for corporate tax cuts. Why not? He is their friend.
The answer to the hon. member is that what we need to stimulate the automobile industry in Canada is parity of prices with the United States so that Canadians can afford to buy cars. The leader of our party in this House has demonstrated many times the wide differences between the price of motor cars in Canada and in the United States. But what has this government done, Madam Speaker? It has not done a damn thing.
You have a hung jury on that one.

Madam Speaker, tonight I want to say how much I appreciate the fact that there are several ministers in the House.
On this particular bill I want to discuss those items that deal witn the non-deductibility of provincial taxes and royalties, not primarily on the question that a buck is a buck, which is the fight over a dollar between the two levels of government, but because this particular part of the bill attacks what we call the federal system, and it has put that in great danger. My remarks are not going to be for the purpose of exacerbating this war between the provinces and the federal government, but rather to see if I cannot put forward one or two proposals which point out to governments on both sides of this eyeball to eyeball confrontation that there is light at the end of the tunnel.
We must seek to save our traditional way of operating in the federal system, namely, by consultation, and at the same time achieve for the provinces and the federal government some of what they want in the material sense and in the economic sense.
I do not think I would be accused of being partisan if I were to say that this part of the bill is bad. Not only is it bad in hindsight or looking to the future, it is bad in the constitutional sense, and in the sense that it attacks the traditional Canadian way of consulting our opponents. Further, it is bad for the country in an economic sense.
We are endangering three or four of our most productive industries which have watched the two levels of governments engaged in a war since September, 1973. This war gets hotter and hotter as it forces the companies to sit and wait until they are wiped out, one after the other. This affects not only the owners of the companies but also the workers. Men in my constituency who have been out of work for two weeks are appealing to the two levels of

January 30, 1975
Income Tax
government to come together and resolve their differences. I am not talking just about the oil industry but about all resource industries. The mining industry, which was a bulwark in the past, is being openly threatened by the failure of the two levels of government to settle their differences.
To put my remarks into perspective, I know that since World War II federal administrations in Canada have appealed to the provinces at least to tax resource industries a little bit harder. The figures are available which show the level at which the resource industries have been taxed in comparison with other industries.
In the tax reforms of 1970 the federal government announced it was going to withdraw slowly from the corporation tax to a new level, to give the provinces more room to take more taxes out of the resource industries. Generally speaking, the provinces did not do anything. However, in 1973-74 with rising metal prices throughout the world as well as the rising oil prices, the provinces suddenly leaped into action and gave us a tax level of 45 to 55 per cent. That would be a good round figure. That meant a tremendous increase, tripling or quadrupling the tax liability of the resource industries in our provinces.
In Ontario, for example, the mining tax was boosted to 40 per cent. In April, 1974, and again on November 18 in this budget we are now dealing with, the federal government struck back by saying these provincial taxes or royalties are not going to be deductible under this bill, and that we are going back to the 50 per cent rate.
It does not require a great deal of mathematical ability to understand that if a province has a 40 or 45 per cent tax rate and the federal government adds on another 50 per cent tax rate, you have a tax liability in almost every province in Canada today with basic resource industries of 80 per cent to over 100 per cent. It is all very well for us to sit back and say it is an interesting fight between the two levels of government, but we are talking about a large proportion of human beings dependant on the work provided by these plants.
Second, we as a nation are dependant on the great body of wealth produced by the giant resource industries of forestry, mining, petroleum and so on.
This fight I am talking about has been going on since September, 1973. We have this eyeball to eyeball confrontation. I suggest it is our responsibility, regardless of political persuasion, to realize that the whole country is slowly becoming aware that this debate between the two levels of government over tax dollars from the resource industry is completely irrational.
Every Canadian instinctively understands that we have waited for many, many decades for the world to need our resources. That moment of time has come. It gives us great leverage in deciding, in our priorities, how much we want to develop here in Canada and how much we want to export. Either way, the opportunity is there. People keep asking, is there an answer to this problem?
If you examine the thousands of young Canadians who would like to build homes, and look at their problem of financing a home, and if you examine the few thousand

young Canadians who would like to own a farm and realize the tremendous amount of capital you need to own a farm in Canada, the same reasoning applies to industry. A few years ago $10,000, $12,000, $14,000 or $15,000 was the type of capital debt you looked at to buy a home. The amount of capital debt you looked at to own a farm was $25,000, $35,000 or $50,000. The same proportion applied to industry. However, at this time $35,000 in Ottawa or Toronto will only buy a very small home. If you have to borrow money for 30 years at 12 per cent in addition to the $35,000, you are going to require $124,000 in interest payments on top of the $35,000. That is the same problem faced by industry today. There you have the situation.
The answer we are looking for can be put forward in the sense of looking at the problem from the point of view of a person trying to buy a home, a person trying to buy a farm, or trying to get into the capital intensive resource industries. The first answer the economist gives is that we have to change our tax laws to give such tremendous incentives to the savings component of our structure that we all save more money, and this will give us the great capital amount that we need to do all these expensive things and reduce interest rates.
There is another way of getting capital, and I put this proposal to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner). That is velocity, in the movement of capital. If there were a way of using this same capital two or three times in the same period we ordinarily use, we could, without increasing the capital amount, get the same effect. My thoughts go to this question of velocity of capital.
I propose to the minister that he seriously consider going to the provinces and industries and suggesting he would like to sit down and put a proposal before them, namely, have them look at the figures he could put down before them. If there were agreement, they could work out a proposal so that there would be more money for both. This has to be a contract arrangement, and it has to be that in the first instance to make it clear and easy to understand for new capital programs or new capital intensive industries.
As an example, if the investor would agree to no dividends, if the two levels of government would agree to no taxes, even a $2 billion oil sands proposal after three years of construction could be paid for in five or six years at rates as high as 10 per cent. To put it so anyone can understand it, if we try to finance a $2 billion tar sands plant at the present time under present techniques of taxation, 10 per cent of the cost would be in the form of operating costs. Capital and interest charges would be approximately 65 per cent for a total of 75 per cent, leaving only 25 per cent for the province which owns the resource, the federal government and the companies to share.
If this same $2 billion proposition were operated on the basis of removing the front end loading charges, the operating costs would be the same at 10 per cent. Capital and interest costs, instead of being 65 per cent, would be reduced to 15 per cent, for a total of 25 per cent. There would be 75 per cent to split between the provinces, the federal government and the investors.
This concept will work in any type of capital intensive industry, but there has to be a contractual arrangement
January 30, 1975

for the period of the contract. In other words, every one has to be a specific deal. If you are talking about the great need to have oil sands plants for the national security of this country and you need one every two years, you could get this rotating capital. You could get the pay-outs in five years. The effect would be that capital which is reluctant to tie itself into these long pay-back periods would come in at lower interest rates, and everyone would benefit.
I have been asked what would be the rate of return you could give to industry if they delayed their returns during the period of construction and the period of pay-out? The answer is that no matter how you twist or turn, using a division suggested by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) that the net shares should be split after the pay-out with 50 per cent to the owners, the province, 30 per cent to the equity, and 20 per cent to the federal government, on the equity side of the equation they would receive from 12 to 17 per cent on their money, which surely is good enough with a fast pay-out.
The provincial government would, of course, get the largest amount, much more than it would get under the present limited share-out. The federal government would get much more; it would profit by the rapid acceleration of capital.
The same principle could be applied to any capital intensive industry in the resource field. With a little thought it could be applied to the owning of homes and farms.
What is necessary? It is necessary for the minister to realize that the eyeball to eyeball situation in which he now finds himself should be resolved. This would place him in a position of leadership in the realm of ideas, which would enable him to get rid of many of his problems. The same reasoning could be applied in the case of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), or the minister in charge of housing. These are issues which require a new attitude to be taken toward the mythology we worship today in the form of taxation.
If we can put forward proposals which are economically viable and morally sound, give rise to this acceleration of capital and lead to lower interest rates, we can extract ourselves from the political impasse, from the disgraceful eyeball-to-eyeball confrontation, and return to the old-fashioned Canadian way of consulting with people and getting a deal worked out. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) would appreciate this.
There is another aspect which I have not mentioned so far. I have talked about new investment on a contractual basis. We still have oil fields, gas fields, mines in operation whose debts are partially paid. I would think the minister might more easily get out of his difficulties if he went to the provinces and said, "Here is the level of deductibility with respect to royalties and provincial taxes that we would allow; we said bluntly in the political heat of the last election that you cannot get away with raising your taxes three or fourfold-that we will not allow those items as being deductible." But, you know, to make a system such as ours work, the provinces must be given some room in which to live.
