If the minister were to put on the table before the mining provinces, or the lumber provinces, or the oil provinces, a figure which would be considered reasonable they could start to work down toward that level. This would constitute a formula for existing mines and existing resource industries, and if, as a result of the system, the provinces got vastly more money, if the federal government got more money, and if the investors got a sufficient return from their investments-I have put forward a figure between 12 and 17 per cent over a 30-year period-it should be enough to get things moving. Above all, costs would be reduced, the ability to pay taxes would be there, and Canada would be a stronger country economically. Even more important, we would be keeping our federal system working in the way it should work.
When I consider the difficulties of the people in the United States where Congress is building up toward mortal warfare between the executive branch and the legislative branch, so busy with the confrontation which is developing down there under the new president that they have no time in which to deal with urgent matters requiring their attention, I would hate to see an attitude of that kind become part of our way of life here.
I would think the minister could prove the quality of his statesmanship by saying, "All right, I see the point. There is some merit in your ideas. I am willing to put these proposals down for qualitative examination. I am willing to check whether industry is prepared to play ball on such a deal. I am willing to go to the provinces and put the figures before them." Then, when the first ministers meet in April it would be a matter of ratifying the homework done by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald), and whoever else wants to be brought in on it.
I would think that all Canadians, regardless of which party they support, would be proud of us if we were to put forward a positive, constructive proposal. And if it were proved that we could make more money, no one could hate us for it. Any time one makes a proposal which sounds as if it is the answer to all the questions one feels like a little bit of a kook. But if the idea is sound, and if the minister does make the effort to approach the provinces, and if it does work, ones does not mind being considered an oddball.
With regard to the other proposal I have made, it is surely in the interest of responsible democratic government that before this April meeting of first ministers takes place something should be on the table. A feeling-out operation should go on. It would be wrong politically to force this bill through with this non-deductibility clause in it because, if this were done, ministers would go to that meeting with their hands bloody from taking up the big stick.
I believe there would be no great difficulty if the minister could persuade his colleagues, who, I am sure, are as anxious as we are to get out of this confrontation situation, to divide this bill so that we could debate and vote on, and see proclaimed all the clauses with the exception of those involving deductibility. I think Canada is worth an effort to reach agreement by the technique of consultation rather than confrontation. We did manage to arrive at some sort of compromise in connection with the
2778

January 30, 1975
Income Tax
petroleum administration bill, a compromise which I believe will turn out to be for the good of everyone.
Could we not consider the suggestion I am putting forward, look at the figures, and try it on for size? I think there is enough credit in it for all the people here-to have come through a touchy situation with a constructive proposal. I, for one, would be glad to give the minister full credit for this type of leadership, and I am sure the country would do the same.
As a party I am sure we would have some criticism to make of the rest of the bill; we would put forward our points of view and, maybe, even vote against parts of it. But this clause dealing with non-deductibility simply challenges the traditional concept of our constitution that resources belong to the provinces. I would do anything I could to persuade a government of any political stripe to take a hard look before adopting such an approach. If the minister would consider this matter over the weekend and see some merit in my proposal from an economic point of view, based on his own hypothetical cash flows, if he would try it out over the telephone or by letter, the hearts and minds of many thousands of Canadians who are dependant on the resource industries would begin to beat more calmly tonight.
I know it is hard for members here to visualize what it is like to live in a mountain town in B.C., and to realize that your mine has to cease operation at the end of the year because it cannot meet a taxation level greater than 100 per cent. Your home, and all the things you have worked for over the last 10 years, will go down the drain because the government cannot wait any longer. Although there are only a few thousand people in this particular situation, they are being driven into the ground and put out of work. Industries which have produced $5 billion to $8 billion worth of products a year, on which the strength of this nation depends, are being destroyed.
I am making an economic plea here, Madam Speaker, but the answer is a political one. Can two levels of politicians forget their eyeball to eyeball confrontation and do something that will give each level of government a fair share so that everyone will benefit? That is not a new idea; it has been done before. I think it would make this parliament stand out in the minds of the people if we did it once again.

Madam Speaker, one aspect of tax legislation and reform that needs more attention and research is that relating to capital gains. It has been recently emphasized that our stock markets have become less and less sound and attractive as a place for Canadians to assist with their savings in the development of this country by investing in corporations seeking to do just that. As a result, this important source of equity financing is falling off.
Lack of confidence in the stock market generally is creating hardships in other ways. Pension plans and mutual funds are being put under pressure increasingly by periodic declines in the market value of securities which they hold, and our tax policies regarding capital

gains are in some ways, I suggest to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), responsible for that.
It is not only the large investors who are getting burned, large investors, for example, like the Canada Development Corporation which lost approximately $40 million on paper on their acquisition of shares of Texas Gulf a comparatively short time ago, but small ones as well.
It is interesting to look at some of the theories of contemporary economists with respect to protecting investors in the stock market. Mr. Milton Freedman, professor of economics at the University of Chicago, suggested-a provocative proposition-that there should be built into all forms of financing, such as bonds, bank deposits, loans, mortgages, wages and taxes, an inflation accelerator or decelerator which would automatically compensate all givers and receivers of moneys, goods and services. Mr. Freedman claims that the most badly needed instrument in the investment community is what he calls a purchasing power security that would offer fixed interest rates plus some compensation for inflation.
Mr. Freedman certainly created a controversy with his theory, and he had plenty of reaction when he claimed categorically that the greatest "bucket shops" in the world have been in Washington and other national capitals where funds are raised through government bonds sold to the public. These governments, Freedman said, sell bonds under the guise of patriotism to help the little man to save, and then tax the investment income, which in purchasing terms has been more than eaten up by the inflation that governments themselves were largely responsible for creating.
The solution to this lamentable state of affairs is, I suggest, in some logical way, to control, if at all possible, the mushrooming inflation with which we are faced today. I am pleased to see that the Minister of Finance is moving toward a partial recognition of this fact in some of the adjustments that he has made recently in the budget. But I urge him to look more closely at capital gains tax theories.
Capital gains tax must be more flexible. Canadians must be encouraged to invest in their own country through the stock market, and it must be recognized that if the Canadian citizen is using his or her stock portfolio on a systematic basis for retirement and the eduction of children this person should be taxed on a different basis, when realizing any profits on the sale of his or her securities, and treated differently than a professional stock trader or speculator.
I suggest that if a Canadian Citizen wants to invest in a Canadian corporation, by definition, and he holds the stock for sufficient time to indicate that it is not a speculation pure and simple-a period of, say, three to five years-such person should be taxed less than a man who buys and sells stock within a few weeks or months for obviously speculative purposes.
There would have to be limits placed on the amount involved, and the type of investments designated, which could be ascertained in the same way as guidelines are set up under the Foreign Investment Review Act to control the influence of outside entrepreneurs. This is where we need flexibility.
January 30, 1975

Capital gains tax, to this point, is used by the government like a blunt instrument, even to the point where, initially, family farms were going to be taxed. It is not enough to discourage undue foreign encroachments in our economy through devices like the Foreign Investment Review Act unless we have a positive side to the policy that encourages Canadian investment risk capital to come forward, and I suggest the government is not using sufficient imagination in this regard.
If I might say a word on tax policy generally and as to when a Canadian should pay income tax, I cannot see the point in imposing an income tax on those Canadians who are, by definition, earning less money than would place them in the category loosely described as below the poverty line. This mythical poverty line is becoming harder and harder to define, but one current definition, I understand, is that it is half of the income of the average family in a given region. When assessing or reassessing what is the appropriate tax threshold or deduction exemption limit, I think the minister should take greater account of what is the real poverty line. It makes no sense, I suggest, to tax people who, by definition, are living in poverty.
Returning for a moment to capital gains, to show how small investors have been losing money on the stock market in terms of actual profit-and I emphasize the words "actual profit"-let me quote an example supplied to me by a very distinguished gentleman in Ottawa, Mr. John Y. Rowe, who, on occasion, has made his views known to the Minister of Finance and his officials. Mr. Rowe makes the point that the erosion in the purchasing power of the Canadian dollar has seriously diminished the attraction of common stock as an investment which, of course, is the same point that Mr. Milton Freedman made.
Mr. Rowe points out that 100 shares of Cominco purchased on June 27, 1967, and sold in August, 1973, would indicate a net capital gain of $272.81, if one assumes that the Canadian dollar has had a constant value. However, it is well known and officially stated by the government that the dollar does not have a constant value, as we all know, Madam Speaker. In this regard we could refer to prices and price indices for exact information. As Mr. Rowe points out, during this period between 1967 and 1973 the purchasing power of the Canadian dollar fell from 87 cents to 65 cents; so the apparent capital gain of $272.81 for the 100 shares of Cominco is reduced to an actual net loss of $536.14.
Throughout history human nature has exhibited, I suggest, that people have a real desire to improve their lot in life by diligent work and savings; otherwise there is no incentive to develop ambition or the work ethic. But the power to tax is also the power to destroy. A capital gains tax without some sort of compensating factor such as indexing for inflation or considerations as I outlined earlier, really amounts to confiscation. The government must take into account the serious decline in the average Canadian's ambition to put money aside and to invest in the future of his country.
Tax policies must, of necessity, have flexibility. They are subject to mistakes and the need for changes from time to time. A fairly recent story in the Canadian Press illustrates, for example, that the Prime Minister (Mr. Tru-
Income Tax
deau) was wrong in claiming the support of an authoritative 1967 taxation study for his government's contested plan to make oil companies pay income tax on royalties paid to provincial treasuries. His office acknowledged that the Prime Minister was mistaken in saying that this tax move, denounced as illegal by the provinces, had been recommended in the exhaustive royal commission report on taxation made by the late Kenneth Carter.
In addition, the Carter report does not support the current federal argument that royalty money should be taxable because the provincial oil levies have become taxes based on profits rather than true royalties on the volume of production. The Carter report, I understand, says that money paid to provinces either as royalties or taxes should be exempt from federal taxation.
I want to compliment the Minister of Finance sincerely on his adroitness in respect of some of the many interesting things he has done since assuming his ministry three years ago.
Name one.

I should not really give him too much credit, but I will ask the minister tonight to consider seriously having a look at a more subtle and equitable way of utilizing capital gains taxation and, I suggest, to take under serious consideration the provocative suggestions made by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) who just preceded me.
I hope the minister will not be afraid to depart from conventional tax theory when he sees from time to time that his policies are not living up to expectations. I hope, for the sake of all of us, that the minister will continue to explore every possible way to compromise with his colleagues in the provinces, for the good of all Canada.

Madam Speaker, it is certainly no secret that the cost of living in the northern part of Canada, and especially in northern Manitoba, is at least 25 per cent to 30 per cent higher than the average cost of living in the rest of Canada. The federal and provincial governments are certainly aware of this as they pay civil servants who serve in the north a northern living allowance. This is paid to practically every civil servant north of the 53rd parallel.
The tax refund mentioned in the budget of November 18 is, in my estimation, only a very small drop in the bucket, because up in our remote area with the high cost of living the small refund anyone will receive will not even come close to meeting or helping to cut down that cost of living.
A tax incentive in the neighbourhood of 8 per cent to 10 per cent for all those people who work in northern Manitoba and the northern part of Canada generally is what is required to help offset the high cost of living. It would also encourage people to remain in the north. Not too many years ago a person could move into the north, work in mining or in construction and make himself a good stake, but that is not the case today. A miner or construction worker can go practically anywhere in Canada and make as much money as he could working in
28626-41V2

January 30, 1975
Income Tax
the north. What we must do is encourage people to stay in the north, making it their home.
We have a high unemployment rate in Canada, running in the neighbourhood of 6.5 per cent. I believe this figure is based on pockets of unemployment, and I am still not convinced that this unemployment rate is a true figure. For instance, I do not know whether it includes all those who are on welfare.
We should be giving the people who are unemployed an opportunity to get off welfare and unemployment, by providing them with an incentive to move up to those areas where jobs are now not being filled. We should encourage those people now on unemployment insurance to be contributors to the tax base of this country.
There is not much hope that the available jobs in northern Manitoba will be filled in the near future without an incentive to the people to move there. Many people would rather stay where they are and draw unemployment insurance. Perhaps the unemployment insurance benefits are too handsome or too attractive to a lot of people. If we provided a tax incentive I am sure we would have no problem filling those jobs so necessary to harvest our natural resources, and really these are the main items in the economy of the country.
As long as the government continues to take the stand that make work projects in high unemployment areas are the solution to the unemployment problem I am afraid we will be faced with higher and higher unemployment insurance and welfare payments. The government now has an incentive program to encourage people to come to Canada from other countries. For example, immigrants can come to Canada, work for two years and get an exemption from taxes. The taxes are collected during the two year period, but when the immigrants return to their own countries they can make application for a refund of those taxes. Why can we not encourage people to move from high unemployment areas to those areas where there are jobs by giving them some sort of an incentive like this?
We must, of course, consider the people who already live in these areas. We cannot bring in people from high unemployment areas and super impose them on the work force of areas in the north. For this reason we must also give the tax incentive to the people already living there. We must make it easier for these people to move to these new jobs. A few people are now moving to northern Canada, but they face untold hardships in getting relocation grants to move their furniture.
If we are really serious about relieving the unemployment situation we should encourage the Department of Manpower and Immigration to speed up the processing of applications by people to move to these areas where jobs exist.
In closing I should just like to emphasize the suggestion that the minister give serious consideration to the provision of some sort of tax incentive for people moving to northern Manitoba in particular, and northern Canada in general, where there is an abundance of jobs at this time. These are not menial jobs but jobs that pay high salaries. We must have some sort of incentive as I do not believe we are living in an age in which we can force people to
[Mr. Smith (Churchill).)
take jobs. There are jobs available today for those who want to work, but there is no bag of oats being held out to interest these people.

Madam Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak on Bill C-49. I realize that we are dealing with concrete facts and figures, and whenever we talk about money matters it seems as though we were talking about facts. But unless we relate these facts and figures to people we are missing the point of the budget, because ultimately taxes mean people.
The proposals that are put before us in this bill, which is a spin-off from the budget, are based on the assumption that they will help to curb rising inflation as well as rising unemployment. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) said in the House just the other day-and I heard the same figures echoed tonight-that since he has taken that particular portfolio government policies have created about one million new jobs. Perhaps he has the statistics to corroborate that figure, but perhaps they have encouraged moonlighting rather than created new jobs because whenever the government introduces new tax legislation which increases the tax burdens, ultimately it is the taxpayer who has to pay those taxes, and pretty soon he will have to moonlight in order to pay the extra taxes. For many this means hardship.
It is a rather cute psychological trick to increase taxes periodically, and then when you decrease them it feels pretty good. This seems to be the year when we are to feel a little better because the minister has included a decrease in taxes in his budget. The fact is that no government can actually create jobs. It can design make-work programs that increase government deficits, which increase taxes, which in turn place a greater burden on each taxpayer. I saw a recent report according to which the government made a $100,000 grant to a company in order that the company might design a new device for a particular industry. The company gladly took that $100,000, knowing in advance that technology was not sufficiently advanced for the device to be designed.
I suppose that government statistics include the number of companies that have created jobs. Yet we realize that no jobs have actually been created. It would be interesting to know whether, when the government quotes these figures, it can also produce figures that show the level of productivity increase as the result of new jobs that have been created.
I wonder whether the government has been compiling statistics that would tell us how much the productivity of the nation has increased as the result of the one million new jobs that have been created. Actually, jobs are created when the government frees the economy so that industry and agricultural enterprises can increase their productivity. That is when jobs are created. You cannot do it simply by printing more money. You have to free existing moneys, and you do that by encouraging savings, making it worthwhile to save money. The minister has taken a small step in that direction.
January 30, 1975

I note that in the May 6 budget, reintroduced this fall, the minister has proposed that a $1,000 interest income exemption from tax be reintroduced in 1974 and expanded in 1975 to include Canadian dividend income. I think that that is an encouraging inclusion, but as so often happens with government measures, it does not go far enough. What we need is a better break on savings accounts so that people will be encouraged to save more money which would be freed to be invested in our economy. This would create greater independence for their retirement years.
It is a fact that Canada Pension Plan benefits are just not enough for our senior citizens, and there has to be some way of providing an additional income for them. Our nation was built and became strong on the concept that to save money was good, and that we should be independent even in our retirement years. But over the past generation this concept has been eroded. Now we need to get back to that concept of saving and trying to be independent in our retirement years.
I wish to ask the minister whether he would consider increasing the amount of savings that would provide interest income so that senior citizens could become more independent, and so that the younger generation would be encouraged to save money so that they might become more independent in their retirement years?
There is a corollary to this, and that is the matter of government annuity programs. A number of my constituents have written me regarding these programs. The first problem with them is that they are compulsory. I wonder about the morality of any program that makes it compulsory for a government employee to invest in an annuity program which brings in a poor investment.
I suspect that there are many members here today who would not willingly invest in a program that pays only about 3 per cent in dividends. Yet there are many government employees who are forced, because of a government policy, to invest in an annuity program that pays only a 3 per cent or 4 per cent dividend. I request that the minister tie the dividend payments to an escalator clause so that those who, by government policy, have to invest in an annuity program, will find their dividends increasing in relation with increases due to inflation.
In closing I would simply like to encourage the minister to continue to break the dependency syndrome and help our citizens to depend on themselves by saving money for their retirement years. I ask him to do this by providing a better tax break and more funds for investment in our economy by freeing this kind of money.
May I call it ten o'clock?

subtopic: TRANSPORT-DESJARDINS REPORT-DATE OF DECISION ON IMPLEMENTATION-POSSIBLE CHANGE IN STATUS OF PILOTAGE AUTHORITY
TRANSPORT-DESJARDINS REPORT-DATE OF DECISION ON IMPLEMENTATION-POSSIBLE CHANGE IN STATUS OF PILOTAGE AUTHORITY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I welcome the opportunity of further debate with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) over the way my routine interest in the Desjardins report has been heightened by his evasiveness. I will try to be objective and fair this evening in outlining what I consider to be a legitimate grievance.
Time does not permit discussion of the report itself, but I am of the opinion that it tends to show that the investigation was a facade. The same ground was covered by Mr. Marler in a report on the same subject shortly before this. Apparently the Minister of Transport did not agree with the findings of Mr. Marler and had the same ground covered again.
However, to lay a brief background, members may recall that on October 2 last I asked the minister when he was going to make the Desjardins report public, and whether changes proposed by the Laurentian Pilotage Authority varying the basis upon which an individual could hold a pilot's certificate were in the interests of safety and efficiency. He replied that he was going to study it, that it was on his desk, and he would make it public when the study was complete. He made no reference to the safety or efficiency aspect of my question at all.
On October 8 I asked a series of questions about policy regarding pilotage, and why Mr. Desjardins' terms of reference to carry on his investigation dispensed with some customary rules of evidence, and was not to be by public hearings. I also asked whether the constitutional aspect of the proposed changes in the LPA regulations was being taken into account.
Did I get answers to my questions? I certainly did not. The minister said we were discussing security not language. While I was puzzling over this, to my amazement he continued and discussed language, the thing he said we were not discussing. He went on to say that he did not know Mr. Desjardins personally, but that he was not a fanatic who wanted to impose the French language on everyone.
With respect, Madam Speaker, I could not have cared less whether he knew Mr. Desjardins or not. I had no reason to suspect that the man was a fanatic, any more than he may have been a circus acrobat or a guru. I protested that I had not even mentioned language, but the minister rambled on and again did not deal with the topics that I raised.
On October 17 I put the specific question to the minister whether, pursuant to section 14(7) of the Pilotage Act, he was prepared to make a finding on the Desjardins report now. The minister replied, and I quote him: "As you know we received the Desjardins report and issued a public release." How was I to know that, Madam Speaker, when it later turned out, by the minister's own admission, that I had not received the Desjardins report, nor had any release been issued? Later, after questioning whether in fact there had been anything released, the minister's

January 30, 1975
Adjournment Debate
answer was no. He said that he thought he had approved it, whatever it was, and then he said, "I know I did something, but I do not know exactly what it was." Madam Speaker, as a member of parliament what am I to make of an answer like that?
Now X come to the part I resent most. In point of fact the minister had signed the order implementing the main recommendations or, I should say, the raison d'etre of the Desjardins report, and he did so a week earlier on October 10. The operative paragraph said:
I, Jean Marchand, pursuant to Section 14, subsection 7 of the Pilotage Act, approve the proposed amendment to the Pilotage Authority Regulations.
Why did the minister not tell me this? Had he already forgotten?
On October 23 the minister had an opportunity to elaborate, if he wished, on the same matter, when he and I were discussing it again in this House. However, he gave no indication that he had signed the order on October 10 approving the main recommendations of the Desjardins report.
On November 17 I had to resort to using a question of privilege to obtain what now seemed to be a very intriguing and elusive report, whereas in the beginning it seemed to be a matter of routine. Even in reply to my question of privilege the minister gave one of his usual all purpose answers, saying in the same breath that "as a government we have to decide what to do about the report" and then "this has now been decided." That was confusing. It was obviously decided before the order was signed over a month prior to November 17.
What it really amounts to is this: why did the minister not frankly say to me, a member he knows is interested in the subject, that he had signed the order implementing the recommendations of that report concerning the LPA regulations? He could have told me that two days after I first raised the matter in the adjournment debate.
Why the evasion? Why the obfuscation? What is so special about this report? Is the minister ashamed of the way it was put together? On the basis of what I have learned about it, perhaps he should be, but I will discuss that later.
If this is an example of how a member of parliament must pursue an interest in a certain topic under the minister's jurisdiction in order to get a true picture, one can readily see why newspaper editiorials across the country are calling for the minister's resignation.
I would like to inform the minister that the basis of the story which offended him was obtained, for the record, by a Toronto reporter who telephoned me when I was sitting in a dentist's chair in Halifax, and I think the minister knows that it was carried in this one paper. It was not a press release. I had no part in its circulation, nor is it the type of phraseology that I would have used. In any event I feel that the minister has been less than frank. I would like to know how frank he has been with the shipping interests which are concerned about this major change in regulations. When did they know that he had signed it on October 10?
I regret this turn of events, and I have considerable sympathy for the great burdens faced by the Minister of
Transport. It is a demanding portfolio, but as a late president of the United States used to say, "If you can't stand the heat, get out of the kitchen". Perhaps it is time for the Minister of Transport, considering circumstances across the country, to consider doing just that.

subtopic: TRANSPORT-DESJARDINS REPORT-DATE OF DECISION ON IMPLEMENTATION-POSSIBLE CHANGE IN STATUS OF PILOTAGE AUTHORITY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in all fairness I think the best way to summarize this whole discussion is to say there has been a large measure of honest confusion and misunderstanding concerning the whole matter. Some people are talking press release or public statement, others are talking Desjardins report, and others are speaking about amendment to the Laurentian Pilotage Authority Regulations.
On Tuesday, January 28, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) took exception to an article which appeared in the Toronto Sun dated January 7. I appreciate the explanation that the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) has just given. That article alleged that the minister had lied.
If one looks at quotations from the October 17 Transport Committee hearings as reported in the Toronto Sun, it leads the reader to believe that the minister was talking about the approval of the Desjardins report. Upon a careful reading of the entire transcript of the Transport Committee proceedings it is obvious that he was referring to a press release on the report, and nothing else.
To set the record straight I would like to inform the House of the chronological order of events. The hon. member for Central Nova put some questions to the minister on October 8 which were answered, and which are now on public record. On October 10 the minister signed an order approving the proposed amendment, referring it to the Laurentian Pilotage Authority. This must take place according to the regulations. The board of directors of the Laurentian Pilotage Authority by resolution finalized the amendment on October 31 and forwarded it for approval by the Governor in Council.
The minister signed the amendment to the regulations on November 15, sending it to the Privy Council, and the amendment was approved on November 19, 1974.
It was on December 14, I believe, that the hon. member received a copy of the Desjardins report, and I tabled a copy in the House on December 18.
I hope this will clear up what I believe to be a good deal of honest confusion about the phraseology and the words used here.

subtopic: TRANSPORT-REQUEST FOR OUTLINE OF NEW POLICY
TRANSPORT-REQUEST FOR OUTLINE OF NEW POLICY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as I mentioned in one of my questions to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) on January 22, we in the maritime provinces have been waiting since 1867 for an equitable transportation policy-in fact, ever since the promise of the Inter-Colonial Railway.
The minister's answer in reply to my question was to the effect that surely I was aware of the special deal reputedly given us by the Maritime Freight Rates Act and

January 30, 1975

the Atlantic Assistance Freight Rates Act. Indeed, I am aware of them, Madam Speaker.
It was because I knew of the existence of these extant, relatively impotent forms of help-whatever good intention there was in establishing them-that I sympathize with the minister when he said the government's transportation policy was "in a mess."
The fact of the matter is, that these have been prime examples of a federal government that uses "ad hoc and bandaid arrangements" in dealing with the economic problems of the Atlantic region. It is little wonder that some of us from that region have tended toward cynicism as we have seen ourselves being almost constantly treated as a colonial appendage in this federation.
Recently, Madam Speaker, La Belle Province of Quebec seems to be joining Ontario in the "We'll control the heavy industry game" attitude. In a power grab that is vintage central Canadian attitude to the Atlantic region, that province is now trying to acquire a new steel plant for its Gros Cacouna port on the St. Lawrence. If they are successful it could mean the economic destruction of a Nova Scotia community with some 130,000 people in its environs. My advice to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson) is to remind them that we in the Atlantic region are fed up with our satellite status vis-a-vis Central Canada.
We, of course, Madam Speaker, are not claiming that the federal government has done nothing for the Atlantic region. We know that it has made a special, even if belated effort, since the middle of the 1960s with such institutions as the Atlantic Development Board, the Area Development Agency, and now DREE. The present Minister of Regional Economic Expansion has succeeded in decentralizing that bureaucracy, and we recognize that he is trying hard to right some of the past inequities.
I must remind the Minister of Transport though, and through him all the cabinet ministers from Ontario and Quebec, that this country and the federal government of it, were one of the last in the non-Communist world to attack systematically the problems of regional disparity through a special agency or department of government. Sad to say, the results are there for us to see, symbolized in the 10.7 per cent of unemployment present in the Atlantic region, as the December figures of Statistics Canada revealed, and they are growing worse.
We still have in our region relatively low per capita and family income, and lower utilization rates of all our human beings as shown by the official labour force participation rates. We had, and still have, an anaemic industrial and manufacturing sector which is supposed to be helped with capital grants and loans from the benign hand of DREE. On the other side, the heavy hand of the Department of Transport allows the railroads to increase freight rates by 25 per cent on many goods moving out of the Atlantic region, and to do away with our special least cost load arrangements which are vital to the small business firms of the Atlantic region.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) claims he was helpless to stop such increases. By admitting his powerlessness against the Canadian Transport Commis-
Adjournment Debate
sion he confirms that the tail is wagging the dog in the Canadian transportation mess, which is euphemistically referred to as a policy.
In the short time at my disposal let me give but one example of how the increase in freight rates affects a small firm in my constituency. The firm is a fish processing one called H. Hopkins Limited. It operates plants in my home town of Glace Bay, which is better known for its coal mines, in Morien, which is a pretty fishing village that is known as one of the oldest coal mining sites in North America, and Louisbourg, of fortress fame, so well known in Canadian history.
Hopkins Limited employs about 100 people, not much by standards outside of the maritimes, but very helpful in an area that is accustomed to trying to survive with unemployment often at the 15 per cent level. The firm processes 400,000 pounds of fish annually and ships it to Toronto and Montreal. The new freight rate increases will mean that consumers in Montreal and Toronto will be faced with an estimated increase of five or six cents a pound. No one knows for sure what the market effect will be, but since, in the economist's jargon, there is considered now to be a relatively high elasticity of demand for fish in these markets, it is possible that 25 to 40 jobs can disappear in my constituency, which already has a very high rate of unemployment.
This is just one small example that can be buttressed by many other small businessmen in the Atlantic region. One would think that such problems would have been seriously checked into during the freeze on freight rates and before a decision was made to take off the freeze.
The freight rate freeze of some 18 months' duration was intended to buy time in order for the Department of Transport to come up with a new transportation policy. So far we have the increases in the freight rates and nothing but a promise of a policy. The minister refused even to outline the substance of the policy which he said in Halifax on January 16 would serve as "a weapon to achieve economic development in the Atlantic region"-.
While we waited for the weapon, which will probably produce yet another blank shot in the struggle against regional disparity, we tried to get the minister to continue the freeze. The minister, however, refused to roll back the January 1 increase or stop the proposed March 1 increase. The Federal Court ruling this week against the CTC now makes a reality of this 25 per cent increase. I submit that it is abundantly clear that the court, in ruling that the Canadian Transport Commission only had the right to approve or reject a request for a rail rate increase, is in fact destroying the usefulness of the CTC.
I think the Minister of Transport has to admit that it surely was an unprecedented step for the federal government to associate itself with the railway companies in their appeal to the court to disallow a decision of the CTC, a quasi-judicial tribunal, established and appointed by that same government.
To this arrogant and uncalled for intervention by the government must be added the ping pong game-

speakeroldname: Mr. Cliff Mclsaac (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: TRANSPORT-REQUEST FOR OUTLINE OF NEW POLICY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I do not wish to take a lot of time reviewing the issue of the freight rate freeze which was lifted and which, as the hon. member well knows, applied to only 22 per cent of the goods moved. It was not really solving a number of the problems which the hon. member, as one who represents the maritimes, is concerned about. In addition the case is still before the CTC. I believe it is coming up for review tomorrow.
I welcome the opportunity to speak on the approach we are taking to draft a new transportation policy. As indicated in the most recent Speech from the Throne, transportation must be treated as an instrument of national, political, social and economic purpose. It must be used to overcome Canada's problems of distance and communication, and help to ensure the attainment of federal objectives such as national unity and national equalization of opportunity from one end of Canada to the other.
A cornerstone of that policy, and one which has been in place for some time, is the involvement of the provinces themselves in meaningful consultation in an attempt to reach a common understanding of regional problems. I can assure the hon. member from Cape Breton that the Atlantic provinces are fully involved in this process. Through the federal-provincial committee on Atlantic transportation we have succeeded in adding the maritime region to move goods by rail and truck within the maritimes, and to tap some of the central Canada markets by selectively subsidizing rates to the tune of more than $70 million in the past three years. This, in all fairness, has to be recognized as constituting valuable help in this respect.
In western Canada, through the auspices of a similar committee, we have put in place or will be putting in place several hundreds of millions of dollars worth of rail, highway, port and airport facilities in order to improve communications and realize the objective of bringing about greater opportunities within the various regions. In addition we are analyzing a whole range of western transportation questions some of which are not peculiar to the west alone. So there is a great deal of study and work taking place.
Officials in the Ministry of Transport, in consultation with other federal departments and agencies, provincial governments and the private sector will certainly, I believe, be able to develop the kind of transportation policy for which we are all looking. They will be in a position to assess the capacity which will be required and the steps which will have to be taken in future years. It is obvious, and I am sure the hon. member will agree, that the answers are difficult to come by-

AIR TRANSPORT-STOL-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF COST
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, a review of statements made by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) to this House on the subject of STOL yields a credibility gap which should not be allowed to exist. It also appears that a very effective technique is
[The Acting Speaker (Mrs. Morin).]
being used by the government to hide the real cost of the STOL project. I take this opportunity to explain my concerns, seek credible explanation, and request a more open, co-ordinated and honest presentation of the facts to the Canadian people.
I refer the minister first of all to statements he made in rebuttal of the claim by the President of Canadian Pacific Airlines that overall STOL costs would be $158 million. As reported in Hansard on October 3, 1974, at page 69, the minister had this to say in reply to a question by my hon. friend from Central Nova (Mr. MacKay):
I think the hon. member wants to know whether Mr. Sinclair was right in saying that the STOL program cost $135 million. Mr. Sinclair is wrong. Is the hon. member satisfied? As I said previously, the program cost $25 million. That is the correct figure, not the one suggested by Mr. Sinclair. I don't know why he said that. Of course, that $25 million figure does not cover everything carried in the budgets of all the different departments concerned.
At that point, an hon. member asked "What is the total?" and another hon. member commented "You don't know." The minister then went on to say:
I do know, but I am not going to mention it for obvious reasons. I am being perfectly honest. I am telling members the plain truth but I am not going to reveal all the details. I repeat, the figure of $25 million which I mentioned previously is the right one. If Mr. Sinclair contends the STOL program has cost $135 million let him prove what he says. I think he is wrong.
Then, on October 23, in the special debate on estimates as reported at page 670, again in response to a question put to him by my hon. friend from Central Nova, the minister dealt with this matter. My hon. friend is reported as saying:
I would like to stop now and ask the minister to tell us briefly by how much Mr. Sinclair's estimate is in error.
Hansard continues:

speechtext: $125 million.

subtopic: AIR TRANSPORT-STOL-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF COST
speechtext:
The minister is then saying that there is absolutely no relevance or accuracy in that estimate of $158 million?
I now refer the minister's parliamentary secretary and the members of this crowded chamber to item 84 of the Auditor General's report under date March 31, 1973. This report was published some 19 months prior to the statements I have just read into the record. The first paragraph of the report indicates some four different departments of government have participated in the project. The third paragraph reads as follows:
The readily identifiable cost to the Crown for the over-all program is therefore about $80 million, but this is not apparent in the Public Accounts because the several major elements are not brought together.
The fourth paragraph of the report reads:
In addition, the government has, by letter to the aircraft development contractor dated October 16, 1972, stated its intention to procure the contractor's products and services for its own purposes and to generate other business for the contractor to a value of $38.5 million during the next five years.
So the readily identifiable cost is $80 million, plus a further commitment in 1972 of $38.5 million, for a total of $118.5 million, and this a year before the Sinclair statement that it was $158 million. It is my conclusion that the
January 30, 1975

Minister of Transport has misled this House and the people of Canada as to the cost of STOL.
What is the true cost of STOL? What is the budget for STOL? Why has this program been fractured over at least four departments of government? How many departments of government are actually involved in the STOL program? Why are the major elements not brought together and presented openly and honestly to the Canadian people and to this parliament? What is the ratio of government servants to civilians who are using this service? Why spend so much money on STOL, which uses over twice the fuel per passenger mile as do modern trains in an era when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) has launched his fantastic taxation program aimed at conserving energy? No other aspect of government has a greater impact on the lifestyle of people than transportation.
I do not have to elaborate upon the importance of this ministry to the Canadian people and to Canadian geography. If I may be forgiven for plagiarism, this important ministry is in a mess. And as in all organizations experiencing trouble and messes, it starts at the top.
I humbly plead, Madam Speaker, for the sake of the Canadian dream, for the sake of keeping this country on the tracks, that the Minister of Transport step aside. It is time for a new, vital and organized type of leadership in this important ministry.

Madam Speaker, I am not going to reply to all the allegations made by the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington), but I should like to refer to some of the words used. I believe there is some confusion over the terminology that has been used in this respect. On October 23 last the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) was asked by the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) whether the alleged statement of Mr. Sinclair, chairman of the CPR, that the total cost of the STOL demonstration project between Ottawa and Montreal was $158 million, and not $25 million as the government contended was correct. The minister answered that the statement attributed to Mr. Sinclair exaggerated the figure by
Adjournment Debate
$125 million. The hon. member will note that I am talking about the STOL demonstration project between Ottawa and Montreal.
The minister again answered questions by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) on the STOL demonstration project, in which he stated that capital expenditures on the STOL demonstration project were $15.5 million as budgeted, and that the total operating costs over the period of the demonstration project were projected to be approximately $9.5 million. Therefore the total cost was expected to be about $25 million.
The hon. member for Capilano, in taking figures out of the Auditor General's report, is correct in saying that the report points out that the readily identifiable STOL cost and commitments by the Crown at that date were $118.5 million. What he failed to point out in using those figures is that the $118.5 million covers all of the costs to that date. However, the only cost in the report attributed to transportation is $15.5 million for the Ottawa-Montreal demonstration project. Most of the other expenditures relate to various other departments, such as the cost of developing the engine, and so on.
Even though inflationary pressures may well have increased the projected cost of $25 million to some extent, the fact is that the figure is not very far off. It is certainly a little far fetched to suggest that these costs could even remotely be related to the estimate of Mr. Sinclair or the figures found in the Auditor General's report.
I am also aware of the very successful twin Otter service between Victoria and Vancouver, and that Air West has taken up options on two Dash Seven aircraft. This is one indication of the fact that the demonstration project has been successful in helping to develop this program, and an indication that this is a good service in the sense that it will assist to return to over-all investment of the government in the project.
